# File Summary

## Purpose
This file contains a packed representation of the entire repository's contents.
It is designed to be easily consumable by AI systems for analysis, code review,
or other automated processes.

## File Format
The content is organized as follows:
1. This summary section
2. Repository information
3. Directory structure
4. Repository files (if enabled)
5. Multiple file entries, each consisting of:
  a. A header with the file path (## File: path/to/file)
  b. The full contents of the file in a code block

## Usage Guidelines
- This file should be treated as read-only. Any changes should be made to the
  original repository files, not this packed version.
- When processing this file, use the file path to distinguish
  between different files in the repository.
- Be aware that this file may contain sensitive information. Handle it with
  the same level of security as you would the original repository.

## Notes
- Some files may have been excluded based on .gitignore rules and Repomix's configuration
- Binary files are not included in this packed representation. Please refer to the Repository Structure section for a complete list of file paths, including binary files
- Files matching patterns in .gitignore are excluded
- Files matching default ignore patterns are excluded
- Files are sorted by Git change count (files with more changes are at the bottom)

## File: .claude/skills/nestjs/references/docs-map.md
````markdown
# Where each topic is documented

Every chapter is plain markdown at `https://docs.nestjs.com/<path>.md`. The full index, with each chapter's first sentence, is https://docs.nestjs.com/llms.txt. Some chapters are long (authentication is ~200 KB): fetch one and read the section you need.

| Topic | Chapter | Package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A first app, project files | `/first-steps` | `@nestjs/cli` |
| CLI commands and options (`new`, `generate`, `--minimal`) | `/cli/usages` | `@nestjs/cli` |
| Controllers, routes, status codes, `@HttpCode()` | `/controllers` | `@nestjs/common` |
| Providers and dependency injection | `/providers`, `/fundamentals/custom-providers` | |
| Modules, `exports`, global and dynamic modules | `/modules`, `/fundamentals/dynamic-modules` | |
| Pipes (`ParseIntPipe`, custom pipes) | `/pipes` | |
| Validation: `StandardSchemaValidationPipe` (Zod, Valibot, ArkType) and `ValidationPipe` (class-validator) | `/application/validation` | |
| Guards, interceptors, exception filters | `/guards`, `/interceptors`, `/exception-filters` | |
| Lifecycle hooks, `enableShutdownHooks()` | `/fundamentals/lifecycle-events` | |
| Request lifecycle (order of middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, filters) | `/faq/request-lifecycle` | |
| Common errors ("Nest can't resolve dependencies", circular imports) | `/faq/common-errors`, `/fundamentals/circular-dependency` | |
| Logger, JSON logs, redaction | `/application/logger` | `@nestjs/common` |
| Tests (`Test.createTestingModule`, Vitest, Supertest) | `/fundamentals/testing` | `@nestjs/testing` |
| Configuration and `.env` | `/application/configuration` | `@nestjs/config` |
| Sign-in, sessions, tokens, API keys | `/security/authentication` | `@nestjs/authentication` |
| Permissions (policies, `@Can()`) | `/security/authorization` | `@nestjs/authorization` |
| Rate limiting | `/security/rate-limiting` | `@nestjs/throttler` |
| Password hashing and encryption | `/security/encryption-and-hashing` | |
| Drizzle | `/data/drizzle` | `@nestjs/drizzle` |
| TypeORM | `/data/typeorm` | `@nestjs/typeorm` |
| Prisma, MongoDB, Sequelize, MikroORM | `/data/prisma`, `/data/mongodb`, `/data/sequelize`, `/data/mikroorm` | |
| Server-Sent Events | `/http/server-sent-events` | `@nestjs/common` |
| Streaming responses (web `Response`, async generators) | `/http/streaming-responses` | |
| Events inside the app | `/application/events` | `@nestjs/event-emitter` |
| Scheduled jobs | `/application/task-scheduling` | `@nestjs/schedule` |
| Queues and background jobs | `/application/queues` | `@nestjs/bullmq` |
| Health checks | `/reliability/terminus` | `@nestjs/terminus` |
| OpenAPI | `/openapi/introduction` | `@nestjs/swagger` |
| Webhooks | `/http/webhooks` | `@nestjs/webhooks` |
| Idempotency keys, outbox, locks, retries | `/reliability/idempotency`, `/reliability/outbox`, `/reliability/locks`, `/reliability/resilience` | |
| HTTP adapters (Express, Fastify, `node:http`) and performance | `/http/performance` | |
| Global prefix, versioning, CORS, Helmet, CSRF | `/faq/global-prefix`, `/http/versioning`, `/security/cors`, `/security/helmet`, `/security/csrf` | |
| Raw request body (webhook signatures), keep-alive connections at shutdown | `/faq/raw-body`, `/faq/keep-alive-connections` | |
| Deployment (build, `NODE_ENV`, Docker, scaling) | `/deployment` | |
| Observability: overview, plans, first project | `/observability/overview` | `@nestjs/observe` |
| Observe SDK setup and options (`createObserveModule`, `instrument`, shutdown flush, log forwarding, redaction) | `/observability/sdk` | `@nestjs/observe` |
| Custom spans, handled errors, custom metrics (`TracerService`) | `/observability/manual-instrumentation` | `@nestjs/observe` |
| Distributed tracing, error monitoring, production rules, MCP server for agents | `/observability/distributed-tracing`, `/observability/error-monitoring`, `/observability/production-rules`, `/observability/mcp-server` | |
| OpenTelemetry, choosing an APM | `/observability/opentelemetry`, `/observability/choosing-an-apm` | |
| Upgrading from older versions | `/migration-guide` | |
````

## File: .claude/skills/nestjs/SKILL.md
````markdown
---
name: nestjs
description: NestJS, the TypeScript framework for Node.js backends. How to start a project non-interactively with the Nest CLI, the project layout and module system, where the current docs are, and the mistakes agents make in Nest apps that still pass their tests. Use when creating or extending a NestJS application.
license: MIT
compatibility: Written for NestJS 12 (@nestjs/core 12.x) on Node.js 20+.
---

# NestJS

Nest's APIs move faster than model training data, so what you remember may be a major version behind. Check before relying on memory:

- Which version you're on: `npm ls @nestjs/core` in a project, `npm view @nestjs/core version` for the latest. Use the latest for a new project.

- https://docs.nestjs.com/llms.txt indexes every chapter. Each chapter is plain markdown at its URL plus `.md`, e.g. https://docs.nestjs.com/controllers.md. Fetch the one chapter you need, not `llms-full.txt`. Find the page in the index rather than from memory: remembered paths (`/techniques/...`) are from older versions; most redirect to the current chapter, but some topics moved or split.
- Nest has first-party packages for most backend needs (auth, permissions, databases, config, rate limiting, OpenAPI, health checks, queues, scheduling). Check them before writing your own or adding another library. The other skills in this package cover the common ones.

## Start a project

In an empty folder:

```bash
npx @nestjs/cli new . --skip-git --package-manager npm
```

Without a TTY (an agent's shell) it asks nothing: it creates an ESM project with Vitest and installs dependencies. `--minimal` creates a one-file app (`../../../backend/src`). `npm start` runs `nest start`, which compiles first.

It also sets up `@nestjs/observe` (`--no-observe` skips it), which sends nothing until the project is linked. Once the project exists, tell the user to run `npx @nestjs/observe link` in it: they approve a code in the browser (signing up for free if needed), and it writes the key pair into `.env`. If they ask you to run it, run it with `--no-browser` in the background and pass on the address and the code it prints. Never write the keys yourself.

Write modules, controllers and services as files yourself (`nestjs-feature` shows the shape); register each in its module. `nest generate` is optional: `npx nest g module|controller|service <name> --no-spec` creates a stub and registers it, which helps when you're unsure where it goes. `nest g resource` makes a CRUD scaffold of stubs, DTOs and an entity class; use it only when you want exactly that, and pass `--type rest --crud` so it doesn't prompt.

The scaffold comes with an `../../../backend/AGENTS.md`; read it in an existing project, along with `../../../backend/package.json` and `../../../backend/nest-cli.json`.

## Layout and module system

- `../../../backend/src` bootstraps (`NestFactory.create(AppModule)`, global pipes, `app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000)`); `../../../backend/src` imports the feature modules.
- One folder per feature: `../../../backend/src`, `notes.controller.ts` (HTTP only), `notes.service.ts` (rules), a repository (queries), DTOs (`CreateNoteDto`) or schemas next to them. Share a provider by adding it to its module's `exports` and importing that module. Where code goes, how to split modules and what to avoid: `nestjs-feature`'s `references/structure.md`.
- Projects from `nest new` are ESM (`"type": "module"`), and Nest's packages are ESM only: relative imports end in `.js` (`import { NotesService } from './notes.service.js'`), there's no `__dirname` (use `import.meta.dirname`), tests use `vi.fn()`, not `jest.fn()`. Follow what an existing project uses.
- Run through the Nest CLI or `tsc`, not `tsx`: `tsx` emits no decorator metadata, so providers injected by type arrive as `undefined`.
- **Never `import type` a class you inject.** Dependency injection reads the constructor's parameter types at run time; a type-only import erases them, and the app stops at startup with `Nest can't resolve dependencies of the NotesService (?)`. Linters and auto-fixers (`consistent-type-imports`) make this change on their own. The opposite holds for plain types in decorated signatures (`Request` from express, `RawBodyRequest`): with `isolatedModules`, TypeScript requires `import type` there (error TS1272).

## Mistakes that pass tests

Coding agents make these in Nest apps whose tests all pass:

- **Sign-in leaks which emails exist.** Hand-assembled sign-in (`@nestjs/jwt` + bcrypt) returns early for an unknown email (`if (!user || !(await bcrypt.compare(...))) throw`), so unknown emails answer faster. Use `@nestjs/authentication`'s `PasswordHasher.verify(password, user?.passwordHash)`, which checks a dummy hash when there's no user. See the `nestjs-auth` skill.
- **`@Post()` answers 201.** A POST that creates nothing (sign-in, actions, searches) needs `@HttpCode(200)` or the code it means.
- **`@IsOptional()` lets `null` through.** class-validator skips every rule for `null`, so `{"title": null}` reaches the database and fails with a 500. For "may be left out, not null", use `@ValidateIf((_, value) => value !== undefined)` instead. Zod's `.optional()` doesn't have this problem.
- **A short HS256 secret.** `@nestjs/authentication`'s `accessToken.key` needs at least 32 bytes and stops the app at startup otherwise. Never hash or pad a secret to fit: tokens are then signed with a different key and whatever verifies them with the real secret rejects them. The `nestjs-auth` skill covers a secret the task fixes.
- **The OpenAPI document leaves out its own route.** `SwaggerModule.setup()` serves the document outside Nest's router, so it isn't listed. Add it if the contract says every route is documented (`nestjs-production`).
- **Stopping servers.** Start a server in the background, note its PID (`npm start > server.log 2>&1 & echo $!`), and stop it with `kill <pid>`, or by its port: `kill $(lsof -ti tcp:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN)`. Never `pkill -f nest` or `pkill -f "npm start"`: they match other projects' processes on the machine.

A contract the task fixes (status codes, error bodies, secrets, field names) wins over a package's defaults. Adapt the package, or say what you couldn't do.

When a task says how to test, follow it. When it says nothing, cover the behaviour you change with focused tests rather than broad e2e suites.

## Other skills in this package

- `nestjs-feature`: modules, controllers, services, validation (Zod with `@Body({ schema })`, or class-validator), status codes, error bodies, Server-Sent Events.
- `nestjs-auth`: `@nestjs/authentication` and `@nestjs/authorization`.
- `nestjs-data`: `@nestjs/drizzle` and `@nestjs/typeorm`.
- `nestjs-testing`: unit and e2e tests.
- `nestjs-production`: config, logging, observability (NestJS Observe), health checks, rate limiting, OpenAPI, shutdown, deployment.

More detail: [references/docs-map.md](references/docs-map.md) lists the docs chapter for each topic.
````

````markdown
# @nestjs/authentication recipes

Full tutorial and reference: https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authentication.md (about 200 KB: fetch it and read the section you need). Imports are from `@nestjs/authentication` unless shown otherwise; ESM projects end relative imports in `.js`.

Everything marked "checked" ran in one app on Nest 12.5.1, `@nestjs/authentication` 0.1.6, `@nestjs/authorization` 0.1.4 and `@nestjs/jwt` 12.0.5: sessions, bearer tokens with refresh, API keys, the context service and the restrictions below.

Contents: how it fits together, the user type, password sign-in, sessions, bearer tokens, a secret the task fixes, API keys, reading the user in services, route options, production, testing, mistakes.

## How it fits together

- `AuthenticationModule.forRoot({...})` (or `forRootAsync()`) takes plain values only: lifetimes, secrets, URLs. It registers a **global guard**: every route answers 401 without credentials. `@Public()` (route or controller) skips authentication; `@Authenticate({ optional: true })` lets anonymous callers in with `user === null`.
- **Credential providers** are your own `@Injectable()` classes extending `SessionCookieProvider`, `JwtBearerProvider`, `ApiKeyProvider`, or `AuthenticationProvider` for anything else. Each registers itself in its constructor: `registry.registerProvider(this, { order })`. The guard asks them in ascending `order`; the first that returns a user wins. Two providers with the same order fail at startup.
- `validate()` (or `findKey()`) runs on every request and loads the current user, so a deleted user or a changed role takes effect at once. Keep roles out of token claims.
- Lifetimes are milliseconds or strings (`'15m'`, `'14d'`). `3600` is 3.6 seconds; a numeric lifetime under a minute logs a warning.

```typescript
// Tell the package your user type once; @CurrentUser(), AuthenticationContext and the providers follow it.
declare module '@nestjs/authentication' {
  interface AuthenticationTypes {
    user: User;
    // refreshTokens: false;  // with `refreshToken: false`, so issue() is typed without one
  }
}
```

## Password sign-in

```typescript
@Injectable()
export class CredentialsService {
  constructor(private readonly users: UsersRepository, private readonly passwordHasher: PasswordHasher) {}

  async register(email: string, password: string) {
    // Insert and map the unique violation to 409 (see nestjs-data); a lookup first races.
    return this.users.create(email, await this.passwordHasher.hash(password));
  }

  /** The user, or null when the email or the password is wrong. */
  async verify(email: string, password: string) {
    const found = await this.users.findCredentials(email); // { user, passwordHash } | null
    // No account: verify() checks a dummy hash, so the timing doesn't reveal which emails exist.
    const valid = await this.passwordHasher.verify(password, found?.passwordHash);
    if (!valid || !found) return null;
    if (this.passwordHasher.needsRehash(found.passwordHash)) {
      await this.users.updatePasswordHash(found.user.id, await this.passwordHasher.hash(password));
    }
    return found.user;
  }
}
```

- Keep the hash inside the repository: everything else gets a user without it, so it can't leak into a response or a log.
- Answer a wrong password and an unknown email identically (same status, same body). Sign-up can still reveal that an address exists (409); if that matters, answer sign-up the same way too and email the owner instead.
- `hash()` refuses an empty password and one over 4 KiB; length and strength rules are yours (validate at sign-up, not at sign-in, so passwords set under older rules still work).
- Throttle sign-in and token routes per IP and per account (`nestjs-production`, and "Rate-limit sign-in" in the docs).

## Sessions (browser apps)

```typescript
@Injectable()
export class SessionAuth extends SessionCookieProvider<User> {
  constructor(private readonly users: UsersRepository, registry: AuthenticationRegistry) {
    super();
    registry.registerProvider(this); // order 0
  }
  validate(session: SessionRecord) {
    return this.users.findById(session.userId); // null ends the session
  }
}

@Public()
@Controller('auth')
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly credentials: CredentialsService, private readonly signInService: SignInService) {}

  @Post('sign-in')
  @HttpCode(200)
  async signIn(@Body({ schema: credentialsSchema }) body: Credentials) {
    const user = await this.credentials.verify(body.email, body.password);
    if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid email or password');
    const { session } = await this.signInService.signIn(user.id, { method: 'password' }); // sets the cookie itself
    return { mfaRequired: session.mfa === 'pending' };
  }

  @Post('sign-out')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async signOut() {
    if (!(await this.signInService.signOut())) throw new UnauthorizedException(); // no session cookie
  }
}
```

- `signIn()` creates the session, sets the cookie (`__Host-sid`: `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`), drops the browser's previous session (session fixation) and refuses a sign-in posted from another site (403).
- Locally over plain HTTP on a host other than `localhost`, set `session: { cookie: { secure: false } }`; the cookie is then named `sid` (checked).
- `SessionService.list(userId)` and `revoke(sessionId, { userId })` for a "where you're signed in" page; `signInService.signOutEverywhere(userId)` ends every session and refresh token. Rotate with `signInService.rotateSession()` after a privilege change.
- Cross-origin writes don't count as signed in. A web app on another origin goes in `session.trustedOrigins`; on Nest 12.1+ also call `app.enableCsrfProtection()`.

## Bearer tokens you issue (secret of 32+ bytes)

Checked on 0.1.6: with a 12-byte key the app stops at startup (`the key is not a valid HS256 key; HS256 needs a secret of at least 32 bytes`); with a 32-byte key the code below signs in and authenticates.

```typescript
// app.module.ts
AuthenticationModule.forRoot({
  accessToken: { key: process.env.JWT_SECRET!, ttl: '15m' }, // issuer and audience are optional, checked when set
  // refreshToken: false,  // bearer-only APIs that make clients sign in again: no refresh-token store needed
}),

@Injectable()
export class JwtAuth extends JwtBearerProvider<User> {
  constructor(private readonly users: UsersRepository, registry: AuthenticationRegistry) {
    super(); // verifies with the module's accessToken options
    registry.registerProvider(this, { order: 1 });
  }
  validate({ sub }: JwtClaims) {
    return sub ? this.users.findById(sub) : null; // sub is a string: convert it for numeric ids
  }
}

@Public()
@Controller('auth/token')
export class TokensController {
  constructor(private readonly credentials: CredentialsService, private readonly tokens: TokenService) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(200)
  async issue(@Body({ schema: credentialsSchema }) body: Credentials) {
    const user = await this.credentials.verify(body.email, body.password);
    if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid email or password');
    return this.tokens.issue(String(user.id), { method: 'password' }); // { accessToken, expiresIn, refreshToken }
  }

  @Post('refresh')
  @HttpCode(200)
  refresh(@Body('refreshToken') refreshToken: string) {
    return this.tokens.refresh(refreshToken); // a new pair; an unknown, expired or reused token is a 401
  }

  @Post('revoke')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async revoke(@Body('refreshToken') refreshToken: string) {
    await this.tokens.revoke(refreshToken); // same answer for unknown tokens (RFC 7009)
  }
}
```

- Checked: refreshing works once per token. Reusing a spent refresh token is a 401 and revokes its whole family, so the newer token from the same sign-in stops working too: whoever stole one, both parties must sign in again.
- Access tokens stay valid until they expire, even after sign-out everywhere: keep them short (`15m`).
- A request with no credentials gets 401 with `errorCode: 'missing_credentials'` and `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`; a bad or expired token gets 401 with an RFC 6750 `error="invalid_token"` challenge, which tells clients to refresh.

## A secret the task fixes

`accessToken.key` refuses an HS256 secret under 32 bytes. When the secret is given (an environment variable with a short default, a value other services verify with), keep it and don't transform it. Sign with `@nestjs/jwt` (`npm i @nestjs/jwt`), and verify through your own provider, so the global guard, `@Public()` and `@CurrentUser()` keep working. Checked on Nest 12.5 with `@nestjs/authentication` 0.1.6 and `@nestjs/jwt` 12.0.5, with an 11-byte secret: tokens signed elsewhere with the raw secret verify, a forged one gets 401.

```typescript
// app.module.ts
@Module({
  imports: [
    AuthenticationModule.forRoot({}), // no accessToken: this app's tokens come from @nestjs/jwt
    JwtModule.register({ secret: process.env.JWT_SECRET!, signOptions: { expiresIn: '15m' } }), // the secret as given: no padding, no hashing
    // ...
  ],
  providers: [JwtAuth],
})
export class AppModule {}
```

```typescript
// jwt-auth.provider.ts
import { Injectable, type ExecutionContext } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { AuthenticationError, AuthenticationProvider, AuthenticationRegistry } from '@nestjs/authentication';

@Injectable()
export class JwtAuth extends AuthenticationProvider<User> {
  constructor(private readonly jwt: JwtService, private readonly users: UsersRepository, registry: AuthenticationRegistry) {
    super();
    registry.registerProvider(this);
  }

  async authenticate(context: ExecutionContext) {
    const header = this.header(context, 'authorization');
    if (!header?.startsWith('Bearer ')) return null; // no credentials: the guard answers 401
    let sub: number;
    try {
      ({ sub } = await this.jwt.verifyAsync<{ sub: number }>(header.slice(7))); // HS256, checks exp
    } catch {
      throw new AuthenticationError('Invalid or expired token'); // 401
    }
    const user = await this.users.findById(sub); // current user and role, on every request
    if (!user) throw new AuthenticationError('Invalid or expired token');
    return { user };
  }

  challenge() {
    return 'Bearer'; // WWW-Authenticate on a 401
  }
}
```

Sign in with `PasswordHasher.verify()` as above, then `return { accessToken: await this.jwt.signAsync({ sub: user.id }) }`. Tell the user the secret is too short for production use.

## API keys

```typescript
@Injectable()
export class ApiKeyAuth extends ApiKeyProvider<User> {
  constructor(private readonly keys: ApiKeysRepository, private readonly users: UsersRepository, registry: AuthenticationRegistry) {
    super({ prefix: 'acme' }); // keys look like acme_<id>_<secret>; the prefix lets secret scanners find leaks
    registry.registerProvider(this, { order: 2 });
  }

  // Called with the id part of a key; the provider compares the SHA-256 in constant time and checks expiresAt.
  async findKey(id: string) {
    const key = await this.keys.findById(id);
    const user = key && (await this.users.findById(key.userId));
    return user ? { hash: key.hash, user, expiresAt: key.expiresAt } : null; // null: unknown, revoked, or owner gone
  }
}

// Managed with a session only: a leaked key can't create more keys or revoke its owner's.
@Authenticate({ providers: [SessionAuth] })
@Controller('api-keys')
export class ApiKeysController {
  constructor(private readonly apiKeyAuth: ApiKeyAuth, private readonly keys: ApiKeysRepository) {}

  @Post()
  async create(@CurrentUser('id') userId: string) {
    const { key, id, hash } = this.apiKeyAuth.generate();
    const expiresAt = new Date(Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 3600 * 1000);
    await this.keys.insert({ id, userId, hash, expiresAt }); // store the hash, never the key
    return { id, key, expiresAt }; // the only response that ever contains the key
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async revoke(@CurrentUser('id') userId: string, @Param('id') id: string) {
    if (!(await this.keys.delete({ id, userId }))) throw new NotFoundException(); // another user's key: 404
  }
}
```

- Checked: a key sent as `Authorization: Bearer acme_...` signs its owner in; on `@Authenticate({ providers: [SessionAuth] })` routes it's a 401 (so is a valid JWT); after `DELETE` the same key is a 401 on the next request.
- `@CurrentSession()` on a key request is `{ keyId, expiresAt, method: 'api-key' }`: log `keyId` to know which key did what. Keys never satisfy `@Authenticate({ mfa: true })`.
- Scopes or per-key limits: store them with the key, return them from `findKey()` through your own user or session shape, and check them in a policy.
- A key in another header (`X-API-Key`) needs your own `AuthenticationProvider` that reads `this.header(context, 'x-api-key')`, looks the key up by its SHA-256, throws `AuthenticationError` when it's unknown, and returns `{ user, session: { keyId } }`.
- Open event streams keep running after a key is revoked: end them (`nestjs-feature`, `references/http.md`, "Ending streams on revocation").

## Reading the user

- In controllers: `@CurrentUser()`, `@CurrentUser('id')` for one property, `@CurrentSession()` for the provider's session (checked shapes: a cookie session's `{ id, userId, createdAt, lastActiveAt, expiresAt }`, a JWT's claims, an API key's `{ keyId, expiresAt, method }`).
- In services: inject `AuthenticationContext` and call `requireUser()` (throws `AuthenticationError`, a 401 under a handler) or read `.user` (`null` for a guest). `run(result, fn)` runs code as a user outside a request: queue workers, cron jobs, tests. It's a singleton backed by `AsyncLocalStorage`, correct across concurrent requests and in anything the handler awaits (checked). No request-scoped providers needed.

## Route options

`@Authenticate({...})` on a class or method:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `optional: true` | Anonymous callers get through with `null`; bad credentials are still a 401. |
| `providers: [SessionAuth]` | Only these providers may authenticate the route; other credentials count as none (checked). |
| `mfa: true` | Requires a verified second factor (API keys never qualify). |
| `verifiedEmail: true` | Requires `emailVerified`; 403 `email_unverified` otherwise. |

## Production

- Stores: sessions, refresh tokens and the other features' state live in memory until you register a store (`AuthenticationStorage.registerSource()` with `sessions`, `refreshTokens`, `mfa`, `magicLinks`, `oidcStates`, `emailTokens`). With `NODE_ENV=production` the module refuses to start on in-memory stores that a configured feature uses. The docs' "Keep sessions and tokens in your database" builds a Drizzle store and ships contract tests to run against yours.
- Audit: `AuthenticationEvents.events$` (and diagnostics channels `nestjs:authentication:<type>`) emits `sign-in`, `sign-out`, `refresh-token-reused`, `mfa-failed`, `password-reset-requested` and more. Alert on `refresh-token-reused`.
- Secrets from a secret manager; HTTPS (the session cookie is `Secure`); `trustedOrigins` for a web app on another origin.

## Testing

- `.overrideProvider(PasswordHasher).useValue(new PasswordHasher({ logN: 10 }))`: the default cost is ~0.3 s and 128 MiB per hash.
- Sign a test user in without the sign-in route: `await app.get(TokenService).issue(user.id)` returns a bearer token; `SessionService.create()` a session cookie (checked for tokens).
- Run service code as a user without HTTP: `app.get(AuthenticationContext).run({ user }, () => service.create(...))` (checked).
- Keep one e2e test that signs in through the real route and calls a protected one: it catches a wrong guard order or a provider that never registered.

## Mistakes

- Returning early for an unknown email (`if (!user) throw`) before checking the password: the timing reveals which emails exist.
- `@Post()` sign-in without `@HttpCode(200)`.
- Hashing, padding or deriving a 32-byte key from a short secret: tokens no longer verify with the configured secret.
- Putting roles or permissions in token claims, then trusting them after they change.
- Forgetting `@Public()` on sign-up/sign-in (every route is closed by default), or putting it on a whole controller that also has private routes.
- Checking keys or tokens with `===` instead of the package's constant-time comparison; storing keys or refresh tokens in plaintext.
````

## File: .claude/skills/nestjs-auth/references/authorization.md
````markdown
# @nestjs/authorization recipes

Tutorial and reference: https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authorization.md. Everything marked "checked" ran on Nest 12.5.1 with `@nestjs/authorization` 0.1.4 and `@nestjs/authentication` 0.1.6.

Contents: register, policies, `before()`, policies with services, route checks, record checks in services, 401 or 403, errors and events, another authentication, testing, production.

## Register

```typescript
@Module({
  imports: [
    AuthenticationModule.forRoot({ ... }), // first: its guard sets the user that authorization reads
    AuthorizationModule.forRoot(),          // global module + global guard
    NotesModule,
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}
```

- Global guards run in the order modules are scanned. With `AuthenticationModule` second, the app refuses to start.
- **Deny by default** (checked): a handler with no `@Can()`, `@Can.Anyone()` or `@Public()` answers 403 to a signed-in user (401 to a guest), and the startup log lists every such handler: `AuthorizationGuard denies every call to AuthController.me, ...: they declare no check`. Read that line after adding the module: it's the list of routes you just closed.

## Policies

```typescript
import { Policy, type PolicyBefore } from '@nestjs/authorization';

@Policy()
export class NotePolicy implements PolicyBefore<User> {
  constructor(private readonly quotas: QuotaService) {} // a policy is a provider: it can inject services

  // Runs ahead of every ability of this policy, on routes and in services alike.
  before(user: User | null) {
    if (user?.role === 'admin') return true; // true allows, false denies, nothing lets the ability decide
  }

  // Route abilities: the guard has no record, and may have a guest (null).
  create(user: User | null) {
    return !!user;
  }

  // Record abilities: called from the service with the record.
  edit(user: User, note: Note) {
    return note.ownerId === user.id;
  }

  // Abilities may be async; guard, authorize() and can() await them.
  async createMore(user: User, current: number) {
    return current < (await this.quotas.maxNotesFor(user));
  }
}
```

- An ability's first parameter is the user; it returns `boolean` or `Promise<boolean>`, and only a literal `true` allows.
- Register the policy in its feature module's `providers` with the services it injects; `@Policy()` makes it injectable and the module finds it anywhere.
- Policies must be singletons: a request-scoped policy, or one depending on a request-scoped provider, throws at startup. Pass per-request facts as arguments.
- `before()` skips every ability of its policy, including rules that should bind admins too ("nobody refunds a shipped order"). For those, check the ability name `before()` receives, or keep them in a policy without a bypass.
- Checked: with `before()` above, an admin creates past the quota (`createMore` never runs) and edits other users' notes; a user over the quota gets 403.

## Route checks

```typescript
@Controller('notes')
export class NotesController {
  @Post()
  @Can(NotePolicy, 'create') // the guard calls create(user) before the handler
  create(@Body({ schema: createNoteSchema }) body: CreateNote) { ... }

  @Get()
  @Can.Anyone() // anyone authentication lets through; the service decides what each caller sees
  list() { ... }

  // viewNotesOf(user: User | null, userId: string) in the policy: the third argument supplies userId
  @Get('users/:userId/notes')
  @Can(NotePolicy, 'viewNotesOf', (context) => [context.switchToHttp().getRequest().params.userId])
  listFor(@Param('userId') userId: string) { ... }
}
```

- `@Can()` is type-checked: a misspelt ability, or one that needs a record, doesn't compile on a route.
- The argument function runs in the guard, before pipes: params are raw strings. Pass ids, not records (loading the record in the guard loads it twice and answers 403 before the handler can answer 404).
- `@Can()` on the class applies to every method; `@Can.Anyone()` or `@Public()` on a method lifts it there.

## Record checks in services

```typescript
@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  constructor(private readonly authorization: AuthorizationService, private readonly context: AuthenticationContext) {}

  async edit(id: string, changes: UpdateNote) {
    const user = this.context.requireUser();
    const note = await this.repository.findById(id);
    if (!note) throw new NotFoundException();                          // 404 first
    await this.authorization.authorize(NotePolicy, 'edit', user, note); // 403 (401 for a guest) when denied
    return this.repository.update(id, changes);
  }

  async list() {
    const user = this.context.requireUser();
    const notes = await this.repository.findVisibleTo(user); // filter in the query, not by checking every row
    return Promise.all(notes.map(async (note) => ({ ...note, canEdit: await this.authorization.can(NotePolicy, 'edit', user, note) })));
  }
}
```

- `authorize()` throws on a denial; `can()` resolves to `true` or `false` and never throws. Checked: `can()` flags come out per row (`one:true`, `admin0:false`).
- Each `can()` flag runs the ability once per row, async work included: cache slow lookups (limits, plans) per request.
- Re-check state when you write: two requests can both pass `authorize()` on a `paid` order. Make the write conditional (`UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'paid'`).
- Where existence is sensitive (sequential ids, other users' records), answer 404 instead of 403: scope the query by owner, so someone else's record is simply not found.

## 401 or 403

| Caller | Status | From |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No or bad credentials on a route that needs a user | 401 (`WWW-Authenticate`) | authentication, before any policy |
| Guest on an optional route, policy denies `null` | 401 | authorization: signing in might change the answer |
| Signed-in user, policy denies | 403 | authorization |

## Errors and events

- `authorize()` throws `AuthorizationError` (`reason: 'unauthenticated' | 'forbidden'`, `status`, `policy`, `ability`). Leaving a handler, it becomes `UnauthorizedException`/`ForbiddenException`, so a global exception filter shapes it. Thrown in your own guard or middleware, it isn't mapped and becomes a 500: use `can()` there.
- The 403 body doesn't name the ability. To know which check refused whom, subscribe to `AuthorizationEvents.events$` (checked: `forbidden:NotePolicy.createMore`, `forbidden:NotePolicy.administer`; guests stopped by authentication emit nothing here). `can()` returning `false` isn't a denial and emits nothing.

```typescript
@Injectable()
export class DenialLog implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(DenialLog.name);
  constructor(private readonly events: AuthorizationEvents) {}
  onModuleInit() {
    this.events.events$.subscribe((e) => this.logger.warn('Denied', { policy: e.policy, ability: e.ability, reason: e.reason, userId: (e.user as User | null)?.id }));
  }
}
```

## Another authentication

- The guard reads the user from `request.user` (and the equivalents for WebSockets, microservices and GraphQL). With another authentication guard (Passport's `AuthGuard()`, your own), register it as `APP_GUARD` in a module imported before `AuthorizationModule`, never with `app.useGlobalGuards()` (those run after every `APP_GUARD`); the order check only goes by class names there, so it logs instead of refusing to start.
- User elsewhere: `AuthorizationModule.forRoot({ getUser: (context) => ... })`. Authentication with `@UseGuards()` per route: `forRoot({ globalGuard: false })` and `@UseGuards(MyAuthGuard, AuthorizationGuard)`.

## Testing

```typescript
// Unit: a policy is a plain class. Calling an ability directly skips before(); test before() on its own.
const quotas = new QuotaService();
const policy = new NotePolicy(quotas);
vi.spyOn(quotas, 'maxNotesFor').mockResolvedValue(1);
expect(await policy.createMore(alice, 0)).toBe(true);
expect(await policy.createMore(alice, 1)).toBe(false);
expect(policy.before({ ...alice, role: 'admin' })).toBe(true);

// Service: the real policy and module, no HTTP. A denial stays an AuthorizationError outside a handler.
const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
  imports: [AuthorizationModule.forRoot()],
  providers: [
    NotesService,
    NotePolicy,
    { provide: QuotaService, useValue: { maxNotesFor: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(0) } },
    { provide: AuthenticationContext, useValue: { requireUser: () => alice } },
  ],
}).compile();
await expect(moduleRef.get(NotesService).create('x')).rejects.toMatchObject({ reason: 'forbidden', ability: 'createMore' });
```

Checked with Vitest on the scaffold's config. End-to-end, sign in through the real route and check one allowed and one denied request per rule; `.overrideProvider(NotePolicy).useValue(...)` replaces a policy everywhere at once.

## Production

- Review every `@Can.Anyone()`: it opens the route to everyone authentication lets through, so its service must authorize.
- Don't cache responses by URL on routes that check records: `CacheInterceptor` answers before the handler, so it would serve one user's record to another without asking the policy.
- Hybrid apps: `connectMicroservice(..., { inheritAppConfig: true })`, or `@Can()` on message handlers isn't enforced.
- Put record checks in services, not controllers, so HTTP handlers, resolvers and queue workers share them.
````

## File: .claude/skills/nestjs-auth/SKILL.md
````markdown
---
name: nestjs-auth
description: Sign-in, sessions, bearer tokens, API keys and permissions in a NestJS application with the first-party @nestjs/authentication and @nestjs/authorization packages - timing-safe password checks, a global guard with @Public(), policies with @Can(), and what to do when a task fixes the JWT secret or token format. Use when adding or changing authentication or authorization in a NestJS application.
license: MIT
---

# Authentication and authorization in NestJS

Use the first-party packages rather than assembling auth from `@nestjs/jwt`, Passport and bcrypt:

```bash
npm i @nestjs/authentication @nestjs/authorization
```

- `@nestjs/authentication` (docs: https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authentication.md): a global guard that puts every route behind sign-in, `@Public()` to open one, `@Authenticate({ optional: true })`, `@CurrentUser()`, `PasswordHasher` (scrypt), sessions, `TokenService` (JWT access + rotating refresh tokens), `ApiKeyProvider`, TOTP, magic links, OIDC. No third-party dependencies.
- `@nestjs/authorization` (docs: https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authorization.md): policies as providers, `@Can(Policy, 'ability')` on routes, `AuthorizationService.authorize()` in services. Denies a route that declares no check.

## Rules that matter

- **Check passwords with `PasswordHasher.verify(password, found?.passwordHash)`**, and only then decide. With no user it checks a dummy hash, so an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password. Never `if (!user) throw` before the hash check: the faster answer tells anyone which emails are registered. Hash with `passwordHasher.hash()`; inject `PasswordHasher` (the module provides it).
- **Sign-in is `@Post()` + `@HttpCode(200)`**: it creates nothing, so not 201.
- **`accessToken.key` must be at least 32 bytes** for HS256 (`openssl rand -base64 32`); a shorter one stops the app at startup. Never hash, pad or derive a longer key from a short secret: tokens are then signed with a different key, and anything that verifies them with the configured secret rejects them.
- **When the task fixes the secret or the token format** (a given `JWT_SECRET`, a default value, tokens other services verify), keep it exactly. If it's under 32 bytes, sign and verify with `@nestjs/jwt` using that secret, and plug verification into `@nestjs/authentication` as your own `AuthenticationProvider`, so the global guard, `@Public()` and `@CurrentUser()` still work. Say in your summary that the secret is too short for production. Code: [references/authentication.md](references/authentication.md#a-secret-the-task-fixes).
- **Refresh tokens rotate and detect theft.** `TokenService.refresh()` spends each refresh token; a reused one is a 401 and revokes its whole family, so the client must sign in again. Access tokens stay valid until they expire: keep `ttl` short.
- **Services read the user from `AuthenticationContext`** (`requireUser()`), a singleton backed by `AsyncLocalStorage`: no request-scoped providers, and `run({ user }, fn)` for workers and tests.
- **Load the user on every request** in the provider's `validate()`/`authenticate()`, and read roles from it, not from token claims: a role change or a deleted user then takes effect at once.
- **Global guards run in import order**: import `AuthenticationModule` before `AuthorizationModule` (the app refuses to start otherwise). A custom guard that sets `request.user` goes in as `APP_GUARD` before `AuthorizationModule`.
- **`@nestjs/authorization` denies every route that declares nothing**: once `AuthorizationModule` is imported, a signed-in user gets 403 on any handler without `@Can()`, `@Can.Anyone()` or `@Public()` (the startup log lists them). Adding it to an existing app, put `@Can.Anyone()` on routes any signed-in user may call (e.g. `GET /me`, the user's own resources) and re-test them.
- **401 vs 403**: no or bad credentials is 401 (the guard's), signed in but not allowed is 403 (`@Can()` or `ForbiddenException`).
- **Streams authenticate once.** An open SSE or WebSocket connection keeps its user after the token, API key or session is revoked, or the user is deleted. It is easy to miss. End the stream when its credential is revoked: `takeUntil()` on a revocation signal, shown in `nestjs-feature`'s `references/http.md`.
- **Response bodies.** The guard's 401 is an `HttpException` (`{ statusCode, message, errorCode }` plus a `WWW-Authenticate` header): a global exception filter can reshape it like any other error.
- **Cost.** At its default cost a hash takes ~0.3 s and 128 MiB, on the libuv threadpool. Tests override it: `.overrideProvider(PasswordHasher).useValue(new PasswordHasher({ logN: 10 }))`. Throttle sign-in (`nestjs-production`).
- **In-memory stores.** Sessions and refresh tokens live in memory until you register a store, and with `NODE_ENV=production` the module refuses to start that way. A bearer-only API can turn refresh tokens off: `refreshToken: false`.

## Pick the setup

| The app needs | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Bearer JWTs it issues itself, secret up to you | `accessToken` options + `JwtBearerProvider` + `TokenService.issue()` |
| A secret or token format fixed by the task | `@nestjs/jwt` + your own `AuthenticationProvider` |
| Browser sessions | `SessionCookieProvider` + `SignInService.signIn()` |
| Keys for scripts and partners | `ApiKeyProvider` (keys `prefix_<id>_<secret>`, stored as SHA-256) or your own provider for another header; manage keys only from a session (`@Authenticate({ providers: [SessionAuth] })`), so a leaked key can't mint more |
| Roles or ownership checks | `@nestjs/authorization` policies |

Code for each row, checked against `@nestjs/authentication` 0.1.6 and `@nestjs/authorization` 0.1.4: [references/authentication.md](references/authentication.md), [references/authorization.md](references/authorization.md).
````

## File: .claude/skills/nestjs-data/references/data.md
````markdown
# Data recipes

Every snippet here was run on Nest 12.5.1, with `@nestjs/drizzle` 0.0.2, `drizzle-orm` and `drizzle-kit` 1.0.0-rc and `@libsql/client` 0.18, and with `@nestjs/typeorm` 12.0.3, `typeorm` 1.1.3 and `better-sqlite3` 12 (TypeORM 1.1 wants `better-sqlite3@^12`). Docs: https://docs.nestjs.com/data/drizzle.md, https://docs.nestjs.com/data/typeorm.md

Contents: Drizzle (schema, relations, registration with migrations, a repository with paging and 409s, transactions, migrations), TypeORM (entities, the same repository, transactions, migrations), and rules for both.

## Drizzle

```bash
npm i @nestjs/drizzle drizzle-orm@rc @libsql/client
npm i -D drizzle-kit@rc
```

Drizzle v1 is published under the `rc` tag; its docs and these recipes are for v1. Other drivers work the same way: install the driver and import `drizzle` from its entry point (`drizzle-orm/node-postgres` with `connection: process.env.DATABASE_URL`, `drizzle-orm/better-sqlite3`, `drizzle-orm/pglite`, ...).

### Schema and relations

```typescript
// src/db/schema.ts
import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { index, integer, sqliteTable, text } from 'drizzle-orm/sqlite-core';

export const users = sqliteTable('users', {
  id: integer().primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  email: text().notNull().unique(), // the database enforces it: see 409s below
});

export const notes = sqliteTable(
  'notes',
  {
    id: integer().primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
    userId: integer('user_id').notNull().references(() => users.id, { onDelete: 'cascade' }),
    title: text().notNull(),
    createdAt: integer('created_at', { mode: 'timestamp_ms' }).notNull().default(sql`(unixepoch() * 1000)`),
  },
  (t) => [index('notes_user_id_idx').on(t.userId, t.id)], // serves "this user's notes, by id"
);

export type Note = typeof notes.$inferSelect;
export type NewNote = typeof notes.$inferInsert;
```

```typescript
// src/db/relations.ts: only for relational queries (db.query...); foreign keys come from references()
import { defineRelations } from 'drizzle-orm';
import * as schema from './schema.js';

export const relations = defineRelations(schema, (r) => ({
  users: { notes: r.many.notes() },
  notes: { user: r.one.users({ from: r.notes.userId, to: r.users.id }) },
}));

// src/db/database.ts: the injected type depends on the relations, so name it once
import type { LibSQLDatabase } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql';
import type { relations } from './relations.js';
export type Database = LibSQLDatabase<typeof relations>;
```

`import type` is right for `Database`: it's a type, injected with the `@InjectDrizzle()` token rather than by class.

### Registration, with migrations at startup

```typescript
// app.module.ts
import { DrizzleModule } from '@nestjs/drizzle';
import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm';
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql';
import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator';
import { relations } from './db/relations.js';

DrizzleModule.forRootAsync({
  useFactory: async () => {
    const db = drizzle({ connection: { url: `file:${process.env.DATABASE_FILE ?? 'data/app.db'}` }, relations });
    await db.run(sql`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`); // SQLite enforces foreign keys and cascades only with this
    await migrate(db, { migrationsFolder: './drizzle' });
    return { db };
  },
}),
```

Nest creates nothing that injects the database until the factory resolves, so the schema is current before the first request. With several instances starting at once, run `npx drizzle-kit migrate` as a release step instead. The parent folder of a file database must exist (`data/` here).

```typescript
// drizzle.config.ts (project root)
import { defineConfig } from 'drizzle-kit';

export default defineConfig({
  dialect: 'turso', // libSQL; 'sqlite' for better-sqlite3, 'postgresql' for Postgres
  schema: './src/db/schema.ts',
  out: './drizzle',
  dbCredentials: { url: `file:${process.env.DATABASE_FILE ?? 'data/app.db'}` },
});
```

After every schema change: `npx drizzle-kit generate --name=<what changed>`, and commit the generated `drizzle/<timestamp>_<name>/migration.sql`. Read the SQL before committing it, especially for renamed columns or tables.

### A repository: owner-scoped queries, cursor paging, 409s

```typescript
import { ConflictException, Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDrizzle } from '@nestjs/drizzle';
import { and, asc, eq, gt } from 'drizzle-orm';
import type { Database } from '../db/database.js';
import { notes, users } from '../db/schema.js';

@Injectable()
export class NotesRepository {
  constructor(@InjectDrizzle() private readonly db: Database) {}

  async createUser(email: string) {
    try {
      const [user] = await this.db.insert(users).values({ email }).returning();
      return user;
    } catch (error) {
      if (isUniqueViolation(error)) throw new ConflictException('Email already registered');
      throw error;
    }
  }

  /** limit + 1 rows: the extra one says there's a next page; its cursor is the last id returned. */
  async page(userId: number, limit: number, after?: number) {
    const rows = await this.db
      .select()
      .from(notes)
      .where(and(eq(notes.userId, userId), after ? gt(notes.id, after) : undefined))
      .orderBy(asc(notes.id))
      .limit(limit + 1);
    const items = rows.slice(0, limit);
    return { items, nextCursor: rows.length > limit ? items[items.length - 1].id : null };
  }

  async update(userId: number, id: number, changes: { title?: string }) {
    const [note] = await this.db
      .update(notes)
      .set(changes)
      .where(and(eq(notes.id, id), eq(notes.userId, userId))) // someone else's note is simply not found
      .returning();
    if (!note) throw new NotFoundException('Note not found');
    return note;
  }

  userWithNotes(id: number) {
    return this.db.query.users.findFirst({ where: { id }, with: { notes: true } }); // one query, nested result
  }
}

/** Drizzle wraps the driver's error: walk the causes. */
export function isUniqueViolation(error: unknown): boolean {
  for (let e = error as { code?: string; rawCode?: number; cause?: unknown } | undefined; e; e = e.cause as typeof e) {
    if (e.code === 'SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE' || e.rawCode === 2067 || e.code === '23505') return true;
  }
  return false;
}
```

- Checked: a duplicate insert surfaces as `DrizzleQueryError` → `LibsqlError` (`code: 'SQLITE_CONSTRAINT'`, `rawCode: 2067`) → `SqliteError` (`code: 'SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE'`). The top-level `code` is generic, so check the chain. PostgreSQL's code is `23505`.
- Insert, then catch the violation. "Look it up, then insert" lets two concurrent requests both pass the lookup.

### Transactions

```typescript
await this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  await tx.update(notes).set({ userId: toUser }).where(eq(notes.userId, fromUser));
  await tx.delete(users).where(eq(users.id, fromUser));
}); // a throw (or tx.rollback()) rolls back; otherwise it commits and resolves with the callback's value
```

Use `tx` inside, not `this.db` or a repository that holds `this.db`: with a pool those run on another connection, outside the transaction. To span several providers, propagate the transaction with `AsyncLocalStorage` (`nestjs-cls` has a Drizzle transactional plugin; docs: `/recipes/async-local-storage`).

### Testing

Override the database: `.overrideProvider(getDrizzleToken()).useValue(testDb)`, where `testDb` points at a fresh file (or PGlite for PostgreSQL) with the migrations applied.

## TypeORM

```bash
npm i @nestjs/typeorm typeorm better-sqlite3@12
```

```typescript
// app.module.ts
TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
  type: 'better-sqlite3',
  database: process.env.DATABASE_FILE ?? 'data/app.db',
  autoLoadEntities: true, // entities from every forFeature()
  synchronize: false, // true only for a throwaway dev database: it can drop columns and data
  migrations: ['dist/migrations/*.js'],
  migrationsRun: true, // apply pending migrations at startup (one instance at a time)
}),
```

```typescript
@Entity()
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number;
  @Column({ unique: true }) email: string;
  @OneToMany(() => Note, (note) => note.user) notes: Note[];
}

@Entity()
@Index(['userId', 'id'])
export class Note {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id: number;
  @Column() title: string;
  @Column() userId: number; // the foreign key as a plain column: filter and write it without loading the user
  @ManyToOne(() => User, (user) => user.notes, { onDelete: 'CASCADE' }) user: User;
  @CreateDateColumn() createdAt: Date;
}

// notes.module.ts: TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Note, User]); then in the service:
constructor(
  @InjectRepository(Note) private readonly notes: Repository<Note>,
  @InjectDataSource() private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
) {}

page(userId: number, limit: number, after = 0) {
  return this.notes.find({ where: { userId, id: MoreThan(after) }, order: { id: 'ASC' }, take: limit + 1 });
}

async update(userId: number, id: number, changes: Partial<Pick<Note, 'title'>>) {
  const result = await this.notes.update({ id, userId }, changes); // one UPDATE ... WHERE
  if (!result.affected) throw new NotFoundException('Note not found');
  return this.notes.findOneByOrFail({ id });
}

async createUser(email: string) {
  try {
    return await this.users.save(this.users.create({ email }));
  } catch (error) {
    // driverError.code: 'SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE' (better-sqlite3), '23505' (PostgreSQL)
    if (error instanceof QueryFailedError && ['SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE', '23505'].includes((error as any).driverError?.code))
      throw new ConflictException('Email already registered');
    throw error;
  }
}

userWithNotes(id: number) {
  return this.users.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { notes: true } });
}

moveNotes(from: number, to: number) {
  return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
    const result = await manager.getRepository(Note).update({ userId: from }, { userId: to }); // manager, not this.notes
    return result.affected;
  });
}
```

- Checked: loading a row, deleting it, then `save()`-ing the loaded entity inserts it again; `update({ id, userId }, ...)` on the deleted row reports `affected: 0`.
- Migrations are TypeORM's own classes, generated and run by its CLI from a `DataSource` file with the same options; they can't use Nest's dependency injection. Commands: https://typeorm.io/docs/advanced-topics/migrations/
- A `Repository` call is async even on `better-sqlite3`, so another request can run between a read and a write.

## Rules for both

- Keep queries in a repository or service, never in controllers, and scope every query by owner or tenant in the `WHERE`, not after loading.
- Read the relation in the same query (`with` / `relations`) or with one `IN (...)` query, not one query per row in a loop (N+1).
- Index what you filter and sort by together (`(userId, id)` for "a user's items in id order").
- Use database constraints (unique, foreign keys, `NOT NULL`) as the final check, and map their violations to 409/404 rather than letting them become 500s.
- Return what the API promises, not the row: drop password hashes and internal columns in the repository, or map to a response type.
- Don't use `:memory:` for data that must survive a restart, and don't use `synchronize: true` or `drizzle-kit push` against a database with data you care about.
````
