  - id: decimal128-spelling
    summary: |
      `mongo/decimal128` stores its values as MongoDB writes them: without leading zeros, keeping negative zero, and only a value a Decimal128 holds exactly. A `contract.json` that stores a Decimal128 value with leading zeros, such as `"007.5"`, is refused when it is loaded with `RUNTIME.DECODE_FAILED`, which names the value to store; emit the contract again. A TypeScript enum member such as `member('Half', '007.5')` is stored as `7.5`, so its contract gets a new hash on the next emit. A value with more than 34 significant digits, counting zeros after the decimal point, such as `1.000000000000000000000000000000000000`, is refused in PSL, TypeScript and `contract.json` instead of being rounded; write a value with at most 34 significant digits. The detection matches a Decimal128 value with leading zeros or more than 34 digits.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{json,ts,mts,cts,tsx,prisma}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\s\S])(?=([\s\S]*?mongo/decimal128@1))\1[\s\S]*?(?:[=,(:]\s*["\x27`]?-?0\d(?![0-9a-f]{62}["\x27`])|[=,(:]\s*["\x27`]?-?\d[\d.]{35,})'
  - id: sql-builder-insert-required-columns
    summary: |
      A SQL builder insert, `db.sql.<namespace>.<table>.insert(rows)`, must now include every column that is not nullable and has no default. Leaving one out is a type error that names the column, and so is a value typed `T | undefined` for such a column. Add a real value, narrowed to `T`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,tsx,mts,cts}"
      matches:
        - '\.insert\('
  - id: orm-create-on-update-only-field
    summary: |
      In ORM `create` and `upsert`, a field that is not nullable, has no default and generates a value only on update is now required. That is a field with `@onUpdate(...)` and no `@onCreate(...)`, a temporal preset with only its update phase such as `temporal.timestamptz(onUpdate: now)` or `field.temporal.timestamptz(undefined, undefined, 'now')`, or a TypeScript field with `.onUpdate(...)` and no `.onCreate(...)`. Pass a value for it on create, or make it generate on create too.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{prisma,ts}"
      matches:
        - '@onUpdate\('
        - 'onUpdate:\s*now'
        - '\.onUpdate\('
        - '\.temporal\.\w+\([^)]*,\s*[''"]now[''"]'
  - id: supabase-for-role-replaces-with-role-methods
    summary: |
      `SupabaseRuntime` no longer has `queryWithRole`, `executeWithRole`, `preparedQueryWithRole` or `preparedExecuteWithRole`, and `SupabaseRuntimeImpl` no longer has `roleActivitySource`. Call `runtime.forRole(binding)` once and use its members: `runtime.queryWithRole(plan, binding, options)` becomes `runtime.forRole(binding).query(plan, options)`, `executeWithRole` becomes `forRole(binding).execute`, and a prepared statement runs on the role with `statement.query(runtime.forRole(binding), params)` or `statement.execute(runtime.forRole(binding), params)`. The detection matches files that call one of the removed methods.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '\.(?:queryWithRole|executeWithRole|preparedQueryWithRole|preparedExecuteWithRole|roleActivitySource)\('
  - id: supabase-role-types-gain-members
    summary: |
      Three public Supabase types require new members, so a test double or hand-built object typed with them stops compiling. `RoleBoundDb` and `ServiceRoleDb` gain `enums` and `nativeEnums`. `SupabaseTransactionContext` is now `PostgresTransactionContext`, so it gains `enums` and `nativeEnums` too. `SupabaseRuntime` requires `forRole(binding)`, which returns a `SupabaseRoleScope` (`query`, `execute`, the prepared-statement operations and `connection`), in place of the four removed `*WithRole` methods. Add the members to each double: take `enums` and `nativeEnums` from `postgresStatic({ contract })` of `@prisma/orm-postgres/static`, or from a role-bound client. The detection matches files that name one of these types.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$])(?:RoleBoundDb|ServiceRoleDb|SupabaseTransactionContext|SupabaseRuntime)(?![\w$])'
  - id: supabase-pg-takes-a-pool
    summary: |
      The `pg` option of `supabase()` takes a `pg.Pool` only. A `pg.Client` is a type error and fails at `supabase()` with `SUPABASE.CONFIG_INVALID`. Replace `pg: new Client(...)` with `pg: new Pool(...)` built from the same settings, or pass `url`. The detection matches every `supabase()` call that passes `pg`; leave a call that already passes a `pg.Pool` as it is.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$.])supabase(?:<[^>]*>)?\(\s*\{(?:[^{}]|\{[^{}]*\})*?(?<![\w$.])pg\s*[:,}]'
  - id: supabase-close-waits-for-work
    summary: |
      `db.close()` on a Supabase client now refuses new work at once on every role-bound client and on `.supabase`, with `DRIVER.NOT_CONNECTED` "Runtime is closed", and waits for work already running, open role transactions included, before it ends the pool. With a pool you passed as `pg`, a query after `close()` used to throw at the call; its promise now rejects instead. Await every role transaction before `close()`, or `close()` waits for it.
  - id: contract-artifacts-restamp
    summary: |
      An extension that writes its own package version into the contracts it emits, such as the Supabase extension, now writes 8.0.0-rc.20. Run `contract emit` once after upgrading so the emitted `contract.json` and `contract.d.ts` match the installed extension.
    detection:
      glob: "**/contract.json"
      contains:
        - '"version": "8.0.0-rc.19"'
---

# 8.0.0-rc.19 → 8.0.0-rc.20 — User upgrade instructions

## Order of the steps

Two changes in this release change storage hashes: the type-alias change (`stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases`) and the re-emitted Supabase contract (`supabase-contract-expanded`). Do the steps in this order, and skip a step that does not apply to the project:

1. Commit your work, so the script's changes can be reviewed and undone with git. Then upgrade the Prisma packages. If the project's Prisma config, tests or tooling load `@prisma/cli-engine` alongside the Prisma toolchain, move it to `0.9.0` (`engine-pin-moves-to-0-9-0`).
2. Rewrite the stored contracts, from the project root, with `scripts/expand-type-aliases/expand-type-aliases.ts` (`stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases`). It leaves a project without type aliases unchanged and says so.
3. Change the contract source as the entries below say: a TypeScript contract drops its `types` key (`ts-types-key-removed`), and a MongoDB schema rewrites the enum members and discriminators the MongoDB entries name.
4. Run `prisma contract emit` (this also covers `contract-artifacts-restamp`).
5. Run `prisma db sign` against every database when step 2 changed a storage hash, or when the project uses the Supabase extension. A database that has not applied every migration needs `--contract`, as `stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases` describes.
6. For each migration that is not applied yet and that `check-expectation` or `check-expectation-raw-sql` matches, run its `migration.ts` again. This is optional.
7. Change the application code and scripts: add `--json` where a script parses a command's output (`piped-output-needs-json`), rename `accessWidening` (`access-changes-rename`), read `meta.schemaIssues` (`schema-verification-failed-schema-issues`), complete SQL builder inserts and ORM creates (`sql-builder-insert-required-columns`, `orm-create-on-update-only-field`), and move Supabase code to `forRole` (`supabase-for-role-replaces-with-role-methods` and the entries after it).

The script path is relative to the directory that holds this guide, which the commands below call `<guide>`.

## Type aliases are written into each column

A type alias is now authoring shorthand only. In PSL, `types { Slug = VarChar(64) }` still works, but the contract no longer stores `Slug` in `storage.types` with a `typeRef` on each column that uses it. Each column stores the alias's codec and parameters itself. In TypeScript, an alias is a constant field builder.

Do the steps in this order: run the script that rewrites the stored contracts (`stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases`), change the TypeScript contract source if you have one (`ts-types-key-removed`), re-emit the contract, and then sign every database.

### `stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases`

Migration snapshots, the emitted `contract.json` and any other stored contract written by an earlier release may have a column with a `typeRef`. This release refuses such a contract and says to re-emit it or run this script. A historical snapshot cannot be re-emitted from today's source, so run the script. Commit your work first so the script's changes can be reviewed and undone with git. Run it from the project root:

```sh
node <guide>/scripts/expand-type-aliases/expand-type-aliases.ts
```

`<guide>` is the directory that holds this guide. Node 24 or later runs the TypeScript script directly; it needs no `tsx`. The script reads and writes files only and needs no database. It rewrites every SQL contract under the root, skipping `node_modules`, `dist`, `build` and every directory whose name starts with `.`, such as `.git` and the worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/`. That includes a test fixture of an old contract: if you keep one on purpose, restore it with git afterwards.

In each contract it replaces every column's `typeRef` with the parameters of the `storage.types` entry it names, and removes each entry a column named. In a contract of your app's own contract space it also removes every entry that no column names. Your app's contract never needs such an entry: it is an alias that the source declares but no field uses, which a re-emit drops as well, or, in a TypeScript source, a `codec-instance` entry that no field uses, which `ts-types-key-removed` tells you to delete. Only an extension's contract space registers a database type. So in a contract of an extension's contract space, such as the copy of pgvector's space in `migrations/snapshots/`, the script keeps an entry that no column names, such as `vector`, and lists it. It makes the same change in the `contract.d.ts` next to the contract. The script tells the spaces apart by the migrations directory: a snapshot that a migration or ref under `migrations/app/` names is your app's, and one that a migration or ref under any other `migrations/<space>/` names is an extension's. A snapshot that no migration or ref names may be either, so the script keeps its unused entries and lists them. The emitted `contract.json` is your app's.

The storage hash changes, so the script renames each changed snapshot directory to its new hash. It rewrites every `migration.json`, ref, `migration.ts` and `contract.d.ts` that names an old hash, and gives each changed migration a new `migrationHash`. When it finishes, it prints how many files it rewrote, how many snapshot directories it renamed, each storage hash it replaced (`<old> -> <new>`), each `storage.types` entry it removed, per contract, and each entry it kept. A project with no `typeRef` is left unchanged, and the script says so. The script replaces the hashes in the import paths of `migration.ts` where they are, so if your project sorts imports with a linter, run its fix command afterwards.

It changes no file and exits 1 in these cases, and names the file:

- a `contract.json`, `migration.json`, `ops.json` or ref is not valid JSON;
- a contract's stored storage hash, or the name of its snapshot directory, does not match its content;
- a column names an alias that `storage.types` does not declare, stores both `typeRef` and `typeParams`, or has a codec or data type other than its alias's;
- a migration goes between two snapshots that become the same snapshot once their aliases are written into their columns, and has no data operation;
- a renamed snapshot directory already exists with different content.

For the first three cases, restore that file from version control, or re-emit it, and run the script again. Two snapshots become the same one when the only change between them was an alias: a migration that replaced `slug VarChar(64)` with `types { Slug = VarChar(64) }` and `slug Slug`, or that renamed an alias. After the upgrade such a migration goes from a snapshot to itself, which only a migration with a data operation may do. The script names each such migration that has no data operation. Delete its directory and run the script again. When that migration is your latest, nothing else names its target snapshot, so the script names that snapshot directory too; delete it as well. The script then writes the hash of the merged snapshot into every `migration.json`, ref and `migration.ts` that names either old hash, and gives each changed migration a new `migrationHash`. A migration with a data operation keeps its operations and goes from the merged snapshot to itself. If it stops partway, for example on a full disk, it says so; run it again to finish.

If you upgrade from a release before 8.0.0-rc.19 and also run `remove-nocheck.ts` from the 8.0.0-rc.18 to 8.0.0-rc.19 guide, the two scripts may run in either order: each checks the hash of the content it reads.

Then re-emit the contract with `prisma contract emit`. A contract written in PSL gives the contract the script wrote, so the latest snapshot, the head ref and the emitted contract keep one storage hash. A contract written in TypeScript needs `ts-types-key-removed` first.

Each database's marker still holds the old storage hash, so `prisma db verify` and `prisma db migrate` refuse it until you sign it. The database itself does not change. After the re-emit, run `prisma db sign` against every database (development, staging, production):

```sh
prisma db sign --db "$DATABASE_URL"
```

A plain `prisma db sign` signs the database against the emitted contract, so it signs only a database that has applied every migration. A database that has not, such as production while the latest migrations wait for review, is refused: `db sign` says its schema does not satisfy the contract, and `prisma db migrate` stops with `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH`, because the marker holds an old hash that no migration names any more. Sign such a database with the contract of the last migration it applied, then migrate it:

```sh
prisma db sign --contract <the last migration it applied> --db "$DATABASE_URL"
prisma db migrate --db "$DATABASE_URL"
```

`--contract` takes the migration's directory name, such as `20260917T0818_add_post_expires_at`, or the new hash that migration goes to. To find it, run `prisma migration status` against the database. It prints the start of the old hash the marker holds: `Database marker <hash> is not in the on-disk migration graph`. The error of `prisma db migrate` prints the whole hash: `The database's marker names <hash>`, or `DB marker is <hash>` before 8.0.0-rc.21. Recover with `db sign --contract` as this section says, not with the error's next actions: the marker is outside the migration graph only because the upgrade gave the migrations new hashes. Find the line of the script's `<old> -> <new>` list whose old hash is that one. The new hash on that line is the one to sign with, and the migration that goes to it is the last one the database applied.

The script has already written the new hash into each ref, so when `db sign` advances a ref, such as `migrations/app/refs/db.json`, it prints the new hash twice: `Advanced ref "db" → <new hash> (was <new hash>)`. This is expected, and the database is signed.

The script also gives each rewritten migration a new hash, and the database's migration history keeps the old ones. After the upgrade, `prisma migration status` therefore no longer marks the migrations applied before it as applied, although it still reports the database as up to date. `prisma db migrate` runs none of them again, and `prisma db verify` passes.

### `psl-alias-attributes`

There is nothing to change. PSL gains two things:

```prisma
types {
  Slug      = VarChar(64)
  UpdatedAt = TimestampString(3) @onCreate(now()) @onUpdate(now())
}

model Post {
  id        String             @id @onCreate(uuid())
  slug      Slug
  createdAt temporal.CreatedAt
  updatedAt UpdatedAt          @default(now())
}
```

- An alias may carry `@default`, `@onCreate` and `@onUpdate`. Each field typed by it gets them. A field may add an attribute its alias does not set, but writing one the alias already sets is the error `PSL_DUPLICATE_ATTRIBUTE`. `@id` and `@unique` belong on the field, not the alias.
- Postgres, SQLite and MongoDB contribute `temporal.CreatedAt` and `temporal.UpdatedAt`, written bare as a field type. Each stores exactly what the field presets `temporal.createdAt()` and `temporal.updatedAt()` stored. 8.0.0-rc.21 removes field presets, and its upgrade guide gives the replacement of every preset. Postgres also has `temporal.CreatedAtString`, `temporal.UpdatedAtString`, `temporal.CreatedAtJsDate` and `temporal.UpdatedAtJsDate`.

### `ts-types-key-removed`

Write an alias as a constant field builder and use it as the field:

```ts
// Before
({ field, model, type }) => {
  const types = { Embedding1536: type.pgvector.Vector(1536) } as const;
  const Post = model('Post', {
    fields: {
      embedding: field.namedType(types.Embedding1536).optional(),
    },
  });
  return { types, models: { Post } };
}

// After
({ field, model, type }) => {
  const Embedding1536 = field.column(type.pgvector.Vector(1536));
  const Post = model('Post', {
    fields: {
      embedding: Embedding1536.optional(),
    },
  });
  return { models: { Post } };
}
```

A field builder is immutable, so one constant serves every model. `type.*` now has a helper for every PSL type constructor of the stack, such as `type.VarChar(64)` and `type.TimestampString(3)`, and for the contributed aliases, such as `field.column(type.temporal.UpdatedAt())`. A string such as `field.namedType('Slug')` named an alias the same way; replace it with the alias's constant.

`field.namedType(...)` still takes an enum handle, such as `field.namedType(Priority)`; leave those calls alone.

A `types` key left in the definition fails with `CONTRACT.TYPES_KEY_REMOVED`. An entry may also be written `{ kind: 'codec-instance', codecId: ..., typeParams: ... }`. If a field uses it, through `field.namedType(types.X)` or `field.namedType('X')`, replace it with a constant `field.column(type.Y(...))` of the same type and parameters, as above. If no field uses it, delete it. Your app's contract space never needs a registered database type: only an extension's contract space registers one, under `databaseTypes`. The script removed such an entry from your stored contracts and listed it in its summary, so the re-emit gives the storage hash the script wrote.

Two calls that set the same thing on one builder now fail instead of the second one winning. `.default()` on a builder that already has a default throws `CONTRACT.DEFAULT_INVALID` with reason `default-set-twice`, and `.onCreate()` or `.onUpdate()` on a builder that already sets that phase throws, as before.

Re-emit the contract. If you ran `stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases`, the column gets the same type and parameters it had, so there is nothing more to sign or migrate.

### `supabase-contract-expanded`

The `@prisma/orm-extension-supabase` contract is re-emitted from its PSL, which keeps its nine aliases. The contract no longer stores them in `storage.types`, and each column stores its own type. The Supabase space's storage hash changes from `292489649ae6d6928de98a32b544bd9caf6b7d49718c10fe2720b83545a4b5a2` to `110ad99e1e466691bdb0a4349a17365561e76ad017f58beb272f4496b05b8e9e`.

A contract that composes the Supabase space references it by id, so this change does not touch your own `contract.json` and `contract.d.ts`. Only the extension version stamped in them moves, which `contract-artifacts-restamp` covers. A database that was signed against the previous Supabase contract no longer matches the new hash, so run `prisma db sign` against it after upgrading. The Supabase database itself does not change.

## The CLI engine is 0.9.0, and piped output needs `--json`

### `engine-pin-moves-to-0-9-0`

This applies to a project whose Prisma config, tests or tooling load `@prisma/cli-engine` alongside the Prisma toolchain. A separate CLI that the project builds on the engine runs its own engine, so it does not have to move with this upgrade.

For every `package.json` or `pnpm-workspace.yaml` catalog matched by `detection`, change the `@prisma/cli-engine` version (`0.7.0`, `^0.7.0` or any other 0.x below 0.9) to `0.9.0` and reinstall. Projects assembled by the `prisma` CLI resolve the engine automatically.

### `piped-output-needs-json`

Engine 0.9.0 chooses the output format from flags only. Before, a command whose stdout was not a terminal (a pipe, a file, `$(…)`, a CI log or an agent) printed JSON frames. Now it prints the human card on stderr and the command's data lines on stdout. JSON needs `--json`.

Find every place that runs a Prisma ORM command and parses its stdout as JSON: `package.json` scripts and shell scripts that pipe into `jq`, CI steps, and code that spawns `prisma` and calls `JSON.parse` on its output. Add `--json` to each such command. For example, `prisma migration status | jq '.envelope.result'` becomes `prisma migration status --json | jq '.envelope.result'`.

A script that only needs a list or a value can read the data lines instead. Fields are separated by a tab and come in the order below. A field whose JSON value is null or absent is an empty field. A backslash, tab, newline or carriage return inside a value is written as `\\`, `\t`, `\n` or `\r`. Paths are relative to the working directory. New fields are only ever added at the end of a line.

- `migration list`: space, name, from, to and operation count, one line per migration.
- `migration status`: space, name, from, to, operation count and status (`applied`, `pending`, or empty when the JSON status is null), one line per migration.
- `migration log`: applied at, space, name, from, to and operation count, one line per applied migration.
- `migration graph`: space, name, from and to, one line per migration; with `--dot`, the DOT text.
- `migration show`: `key<TAB>value` lines, then one `operation` line per operation.
- `migration check`: space, code and where (the path the failure is about), one line per failure.
- `migration new` and `migration plan`: the directories written.
- `migration ref list`: name, hash and comma-separated invariants, one line per ref. `migration ref set`: the hash the ref points at.
- `db migrate`: space, name, from, to and operations run, one line per applied migration; with `--show`, space, name, from and to per migration that will run.
- `db sign`: space, status and contract storage hash, one line per space.
- `orm init`: the paths of the files written.
- `contract emit`: the paths of `contract.json` and `contract.d.ts`. `contract infer`: the path written. `contract format`: the paths formatted. `contract print`: the PSL.

`db init`, `db update`, `db verify`, `db schema` and `migration ref delete` print nothing on stdout; their exit code is the result, and `--json` carries the document. An error in a pipe is now human text on stderr, with the same exit code.

## `accessWidening` is renamed `accessChanges`

`db update` asks about each operation that changes who can read or write a model's data. Such an operation does not always widen access, so the list of them is now `accessChanges`, and the option that answers all of them is `acceptAccessChanges`. Rename each use:

```ts
// Before
const result = await client.dbUpdate({ contract, mode: 'apply', migrationsDir, acceptAccessWidening: true, answerQuestions });
if (result.ok) console.log(result.value.accessWidening);

// After
const result = await client.dbUpdate({ contract, mode: 'apply', migrationsDir, acceptAccessChanges: true, answerQuestions });
if (result.ok) console.log(result.value.accessChanges);
```

A script that reads `prisma db update --dry-run --json` reads `accessChanges` in place of `accessWidening`. The output is one JSON object per line, and the result is in the last one:

```bash
prisma db update --dry-run --json | jq -s 'last | .envelope.result.accessChanges'
```

The question `db update` asks now ends with "who can read and write its data" in place of "who can read and write its rows". A script that matches the question text changes the same way.

## A removed namespace is asked about

If your contract removes a `namespace` block on Postgres, the next `migration plan` or `db update` asks about each model that namespace held, as it asks about any model you remove.

If you renamed the block, for example from `billing` to `finance`, give the rename and nothing is dropped:

```bash
prisma db update --rename billing:finance
```

Otherwise the namespace is removed. A script that runs without a terminal fails with `CLI.CONSENT_REQUIRED`, listing each model. To drop them all and the schema, add `--delete <namespace>`:

```bash
prisma db update --delete billing
```

To keep a model's data, move it to a namespace the contract keeps in the same run, for example `--rename billing.Invoice:public.Invoice`, or put the namespace back in the contract.

A table in that schema that no contract declared, such as one created by hand, is asked about too, by its storage name: `--delete billing.audit_log`. `--delete billing` does not answer it. Another object no contract declared, such as a view or a function, makes the run fail and changes nothing: a view on one of the tables stops that table's drop, and any other object stops the schema drop. The failure names each object; drop or move it yourself, then run the command again.

A namespace that only another contract space declares, and a schema no contract ever declared, such as Supabase's `auth`, are still left alone.

## The schema check's differences are in `meta.schemaIssues`

When `db verify` or `db sign` finds that the database schema does not match the contract, its `--json` output has a diagnostic with the code `CONTRACT.SCHEMA_VERIFICATION_FAILED`. Its `meta.issues` was a list of label strings, such as `"missing: public/users/email"`. It is now `meta.schemaIssues`, a list of issue objects, the same key and shape the `MIGRATION.SCHEMA_VERIFY_FAILED` failure of `db init`, `db update` and `db migrate` already uses. `meta.space` and `meta.code` are unchanged, and so is `schema.issues` in the result of a check that passed.

Each issue has a `path`, the location of the difference as a list of names, and `expected` and `actual`, the contract's and the database's side, one of which is absent for a missing or an extra object. It has an `explanation` with a `text` when the CLI can say more.

In code that reads the diagnostic, read `meta.schemaIssues` where it read `meta.issues`. Where it used the label strings, build them from the issue. A label was the outcome, then the path: `missing` when only `expected` is set, `extra` when only `actual` is set, and `mismatch` when both are:

```typescript
// before
const labels: string[] = diagnostic.meta.issues;
// after
const labels = diagnostic.meta.schemaIssues.map((issue) => {
  const outcome = issue.actual === undefined ? 'missing' : issue.expected === undefined ? 'extra' : 'mismatch';
  return `${outcome}: ${issue.path.join('/')}`;
});
```

The `why` of the diagnostic still lists every difference as text.

## Checks say which object they expect absent or present

Before an operation runs, the migration runner runs its prechecks. When one fails, the error's `why` named the check and said only that it failed on this database. A check that expects one object to be absent or present can now carry that as data, in `expectation`, and the `why` then says what the database already has or lacks. On MongoDB, a check carries the object's name in `object`, and its `expect` says whether it should exist.

Nothing breaks without it. An `ops.json` that has no `expectation` reads, verifies its hash and runs as before.

### Migrations Prisma writes

The PostgreSQL, SQLite and MongoDB operations now write it on every check that asks only whether one object exists. A matched `ops.json`, or a MongoDB `ops.json` written before this change, gains it when you write it again: run its `migration.ts` (`node migration.ts`). Writing it again changes its hash, so do this only for a migration that no database has applied yet. Leave an applied migration as it is.

### Checks you write yourself

In your app's migrations, a check you write in a `rawSql` operation can carry it too. Add `expectation` to the precheck or postcheck step, with `expects: 'absent'` or `'present'` and the object as a reader would name it, then run `node migration.ts`:

```typescript
rawSql({
  // ...
  precheck: [
    {
      description: 'verify extension "vector" is not already enabled',
      sql: "SELECT NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'vector')",
      expectation: { expects: 'absent', object: 'extension "vector"' },
    },
  ],
})
```

Leave it out of a check about data or about several objects at once, such as a check that a column holds no NULL values.

## MongoDB values are written in the syntax of their data type

MongoDB PSL now reads every enum member the way SQL PSL does: by the syntax it is written in, then the casts of the enum codec's data type, then the codec. The MongoDB target has an authoring entry or a cast for every data type except `mongo/bson`:

- a quoted string is `mongo/string`, and `true` and `false` are `mongo/bool`;
- a number is the smallest type that holds it: `mongo/int32`, `mongo/int64`, `mongo/decimal128` when a Decimal128 holds it exactly, `NaN` and the infinities included, and `mongo/double` otherwise;
- the `date`, `binary` and `json` tags write `mongo/date`, `mongo/binary` and `mongo/json`.

A member that was quoted to get a number through the JSON reader is now text, and a member that was written with a fraction on an integer enum is now a Decimal128 value. Rewrite each as the change entries above say:

```prisma
enum Ratio {
  @@type("mongo/double@1")
  Unknown = NaN
  Half    = 0.5
}

enum Level {
  @@type("mongo/int32@1")
  One = 1
}
```

Discriminators follow one rule in both families: the field must be required, hold one value, and have one of the stack's text data types, and when an enum types it, each `@@base` value must be one of its members. A field is text by its data type, so on MongoDB a type alias of `String` is now a discriminator.

An enum on an Int64, Date, Decimal128, Binary or ObjectId codec, or a Double enum with a `NaN` or infinite member, is still refused when a collection the contract manages uses it, because a collection validator cannot list those members.

## Inserts must include the columns the database requires

The SQL builder's `insert` used to accept a row that left out any column. A row without a value for a column that is not nullable and has no default compiled, and then the database rejected it with a not-null error. The row type now requires those columns:

```typescript
// User.displayName is `String` with no default
db.sql.public.user.insert([{ email: 'admin@example.com', kind: 'admin' }]);
// error: Property 'displayName' is missing

db.sql.public.user.insert([{ email: 'admin@example.com', kind: 'admin', displayName: 'Admin' }]);
```

A column is still optional when it is nullable, when it has a default (`@default(...)`, including `now()` and `autoincrement()`), or when the client generates its value on create with `@onCreate(...)` or a preset that generates on create. Rows in one `insert` call are checked one by one, so they may set different optional columns.

For each insert that stops compiling, add a real value for each column the error names. Do not cast the row. A required property does not accept `undefined`, so a value typed `T | undefined` for one of these columns is now an error too: check it before the insert. Rows built in a variable and passed as `insert(rows)` get the same check, so give the variable the row type or build each row with every required column.

### ORM create for fields that generate only on update

A field generates its value on update only when it has `@onUpdate(...)` without `@onCreate(...)`, or when a temporal preset sets only its update phase: `temporal.timestamptz(onUpdate: now)` and `temporal.timestamp(3, onUpdate: now)` in PSL, `field.temporal.timestamptz(undefined, undefined, 'now')` in TypeScript. Such a field that is not nullable and has no default was optional in ORM `create` input, and the create then failed in the database. It is now required. Pass a value for it on create, or make it generate on create too: add `@onCreate(...)`, or set the preset's create phase (`temporal.timestamptz(onCreate: now, onUpdate: now)`).

## Supabase runs every role operation through one object

`SupabaseRuntime.forRole(binding)` returns a `SupabaseRoleScope`, the runtime operations under one role: `query`, `execute`, the prepared-statement operations and `connection`. Run a transaction under the role with `withTransaction(runtime.forRole(binding), fn)`.

| Type | New required members |
| --- | --- |
| `RoleBoundDb`, `ServiceRoleDb` | `enums`, `nativeEnums` |
| `SupabaseTransactionContext` | `enums`, `nativeEnums` (it is now `PostgresTransactionContext`) |
| `SupabaseRuntime` | `forRole(binding)`, in place of the four `*WithRole` methods |

```ts
// Before
const rows = await runtime.queryWithRole(plan, { role: 'anon' }).toArray();
const stats = await runtime.executeWithRole(plan, { role: 'anon' });
const named = await runtime.preparedQueryWithRole(statement, params, { role: 'anon' }).toArray();

// After
const anon = runtime.forRole({ role: 'anon' });
const rows = await anon.query(plan).toArray();
const stats = await anon.execute(plan);
const named = await statement.query(anon, params).toArray();
```

The `pg` option takes a `pg.Pool`:

```ts
// Before
const db = await supabase({ contract, pg: new Client({ connectionString }), jwtSecret });

// After: close() does not end a pool you pass in, so keep it and end it at shutdown
const pool = new Pool({ connectionString });
const db = await supabase({ contract, pg: pool, jwtSecret });
// ...
await db.close();
await pool.end();

// Or let Supabase create and end the pool
const db = await supabase({ contract, url: connectionString, jwtSecret });
```

## `contract-artifacts-restamp`

For every `contract.json` matched by `detection`, run the project's emit command (`prisma contract emit`, or the project's `contract:emit` script) once after upgrading. This entry accounts for the extension's embedded `version` moving to `8.0.0-rc.20`; any other difference in the emitted files comes from an earlier entry in this guide.
````

## File: backend/.agents/skills/prisma-8/upgrading/app/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.2-to-8.0.0-rc.3/instructions.md
````markdown

from: "8.0.0-rc.2"
to: "8.0.0-rc.3"
changes: []
---
````

````markdown
---
from: "8.0.0-rc.20"
to: "8.0.0-rc.21"
changes:
  - id: mongo-contract-target-option
    summary: |
      `mongoContract(schemaPath, options)` now requires `options.target`, the MongoDB target pack, which the contract records. Pass `{ target: mongoTargetPack }` with `mongoTargetPack` imported from `@prisma/orm-mongo/target/pack`, alongside any options you already pass. A config written with `defineConfig` from `@prisma/orm-mongo/config` needs no change.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,js,mjs}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$.])mongoContract\(\s*[^,()]*(?:\([^()]*\)[^,()]*)*,?\s*\)'
        - '(?<![\w$.])mongoContract\(\s*[^,()]*(?:\([^()]*\)[^,()]*)*,\s*\{(?![^{}]*\btarget\b)[^{}]*\}\s*\)'
        - '(?<![\w$.])mongoContract\(\s*[^,()]*(?:\([^()]*\)[^,()]*)*,\s*[A-Za-z_$][\w$.]*\s*\)'
  - id: mongo-contract-input
    summary: |
      The MongoDB type for the object you pass to `defineContract`, `ContractDefinition`, is renamed `ContractInput`. It is the same type under SQL's name for it. `ContractDefinition` now names the plain-data definition every MongoDB contract source builds from, which takes no type parameters, so the detection flags an import from `@prisma/orm-family-mongo/contract-ts` only where the file writes `ContractDefinition<...>`. Import `ContractInput` from `@prisma/orm-mongo/contract-builder` where you imported `ContractDefinition`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?:import|export)\s+(?:type\s+)?\{[^}]*\bContractDefinition\b[^}]*\}\s*from\s*[\x27"]@prisma/orm-mongo/contract-builder[\x27"]'
        - '(?:import|export)\s+(?:type\s+)?\{[^}]*\bContractDefinition\b[^}]*\}\s*from\s*[\x27"]@prisma/orm-family-mongo/contract-ts(?:/contract-builder)?[\x27"][\s\S]*\bContractDefinition<'
  - id: mongo-model-definition-removed
    summary: |
      `MongoModelDefinition` is removed. It was another name for `ContractModel<MongoModelStorage>`. Write `ContractModel<MongoModelStorage>` instead, with `ContractModel` from `@prisma/orm-mongo/contract/types` and `MongoModelStorage` from `@prisma/orm-mongo/family-contract`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$])MongoModelDefinition(?![\w$])'
  - id: mongo-ts-polymorphism-rules
    summary: |
      `defineContract` now applies the MongoDB polymorphism rules that PSL applied. It refuses a discriminator that is optional, a list or not text, such as an `Int32` field (`CONTRACT.ARGUMENT_INVALID`); a variant value the discriminator field cannot hold or that is not a member of its enum; a variant listed in `discriminator.variants` that no model declares with that base; a variant stored in another collection than its base (`CONTRACT.COLLECTION_INVALID`); and, in TypeScript and PSL, a variant field stored under a name a field of its base is stored under, such as the discriminator (`CONTRACT.NAME_DUPLICATE`, `PSL_DUPLICATE_STORED_NAME`), which would overwrite that field; and, in TypeScript and PSL, a variant field that restates a base field with a different stored name, type, nullability or list shape (`CONTRACT.ARGUMENT_INVALID`, `PSL_VARIANT_FIELD_DIFFERS_FROM_BASE`), whose documents the collection's validator, written from the base, would refuse. Make the discriminator a required `field.string()` or a string enum, list only declared variants, leave a variant's `collection` out or set it to its base's, give each variant field a stored name its base does not use, and restate a base field on a variant exactly as the base declares it, or not at all.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '@prisma/orm-(?:mongo|family-mongo/contract-ts)/contract-builder[\x27"][\s\S]*\bdiscriminator\s*:\s*\{'
  - id: mongo-index-shape-rules
    summary: |
      Every MongoDB contract source now refuses an index MongoDB would refuse (`CONTRACT.INDEX_INVALID` in TypeScript, `PSL_INVALID_INDEX` in PSL): a unique wildcard index, a wildcard with a hashed, 2d or 2dsphere key, a hashed index on several fields, a TTL wildcard index, a wildcard projection without a wildcard key, a collation without a locale, and a second text index in one collection. PSL also refuses an index that another model on the same collection, or the same model, already declares, such as `@unique` and `@@unique` on one field. Remove the index or change it to a shape MongoDB accepts; remove a duplicate.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,prisma}"
      matches:
        - '@prisma/orm-(?:mongo|family-mongo/contract-ts)/contract-builder[\x27"][\s\S]*(?:\$\*\*|\bwildcardProjection\b|[\x27"]hashed[\x27"]|\bcollation\s*:)'
        - '\bwildcard\('
  - id: mongo-value-object-enum-check
    summary: |
      `defineContract` now refuses a value object field typed by an enum the contract does not declare (`CONTRACT.ENUM_UNKNOWN`), as it already did for a model field. Add the enum to `defineContract({ enums })`.
  - id: mongo-newly-accepted
    summary: |
      No action is needed. An optional field that a type alias, `@onCreate(...)`/`@onUpdate(...)` or `.onCreate(...)`/`.onUpdate(...)` fills is now accepted, as on SQL; a list that generates a value is still refused. A TypeScript variant may leave its `collection` out and is stored in its base's.
  - id: mongo-prisma6-merged-indexes
    summary: |
      A Prisma 6 schema read by `prisma6Schema()` in which one collection holds two identical indexes, such as `@unique` and `@@unique` on one field, or the same `@@index` on two models stored in one collection, now gives one index, as the database holds one. That contract's storage hash changes. Run `prisma contract emit`, then `prisma db sign` to record the new hash; the database itself needs no change.
  - id: removed-enum-value-questions
    summary: |
      On Postgres and SQLite, when the contract removes a member of an enum, or changes the value a member stores, `migration plan` and `db update` now rewrite the rows that hold the old stored value, and ask about it first. Before, Postgres failed at apply on the new check when a row held the old value, and SQLite planned nothing. If the member was renamed, say so with `--rename Status.ARCHIVED:Status.RETIRED`, which changes the stored value in every row and list that holds it. Answer with `--delete Status.ARCHIVED` to set it to NULL in optional columns and take it out of lists.
  - id: client-members-reject-instead-of-throwing
    summary: |
      A client member that returns a promise or a result no longer throws at the call when the client or the transaction is in a failed state. On `postgres()`, `sqlite()`, a `supabase()` role-bound client and a transaction, `query`, `execute`, `prepare`, `transaction`, ORM calls and a prepared statement's `query(target, params)` and `execute(target, params)` now report a closed client, a failed connection or an ended transaction through what they return: the promise rejects, and a result rejects when it is awaited or read. Error codes and messages do not change. Code that wraps such a call in `try`/`catch` without awaiting it no longer catches the error; add `await`, or handle it with `.catch(...)`. `db.runtime()` still throws at the call, and so does a mistake in the call itself, such as an ORM query the database's capabilities do not allow. The detection matches a file that imports an `@prisma/orm-*` package and has a `try` block, one line or many, nested or not, that calls one of these members or an ORM terminal (`all`, `first`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `upsert`, …) without `await` directly before it, on a receiver shaped like a client: a name ending in `db`, `tx`, a name ending in `client`, `admin`, a prepared statement, or a chain through `.orm`; chains may span lines and take callbacks; leave a call whose result is awaited or returned to an awaiting caller as it is.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\s\S])(?=[\s\S]*[\x27\x22]@prisma/orm-)[\s\S]*\btry\s*\{(?:(?!\}\s*(?:catch|finally)\b)[\s\S])*?(?<![\w$.])(?<!\bawait\s+)(?:this\s*\.\s*)?(?:[\w$]*(?:db|Db|DB)|tx|trx|[\w$]*[Cc]lient|admin|[\w$]*[Pp]repared[\w$]*|[\w$]+\s*\.\s*orm)(?:\s*\.\s*[\w$]+(?:\s*\((?:[^()]|\([^()]*\))*\))?)*?\s*\.\s*(?:query|execute|prepare|transaction|all|first|firstOrThrow|create|createAll|createAndCount|update|updateAll|updateAndCount|delete|deleteAll|deleteAndCount|upsert|aggregate)\s*\('
  - id: close-ends-the-client-not-your-pool
    summary: |
      `close()` on a Postgres or Supabase client built on a pool or `pg.Client` you passed in now also closes its runtime, so a runtime you captured with `db.runtime()` before `close()` refuses new work. Your pool or `pg.Client` stays open, as before; end it yourself.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,tsx,mts,cts}"
      matches:
        - '(?:postgres|supabase)\(\s*\{[\s\S]*?\b(?:pg|binding|pool|client)\s*[:,}]'
  - id: sqlite-open-failure-is-a-connection-error
    summary: |
      A SQLite database file that cannot be opened (a missing directory, or a file that is not a database) is now a connection error (`SqlConnectionError`), not a query error (`SqlQueryError`), in the driver. Code that caught the query error to handle a bad database path catches the connection error instead.
  - id: verify-contract-spaces-marker-location
    summary: |
      `verifyContractSpaces` (from the `spaces` subpath of the migration tools) takes a required `markerLocation`, the name of the target's marker table or collection, which the remediation of an orphan marker names.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,tsx,mts,cts,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$])verifyContractSpaces\s*\('
  - id: refuse-marker-outside-graph-removed
    summary: |
      `refuseMarkerOutsideGraph` is no longer exported from `@prisma/orm-toolchain/cli/control-api`. The control client's `migrate` and `executeMigrateShowPlan` now check every contract space's marker against its migration graph themselves, and fail with `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH` when a marker is outside it. Delete the call and its handling; branch on the `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH` failure those operations return instead.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '\brefuseMarkerOutsideGraph\b'
  - id: execute-migrate-show-plan-requires-invocation
    summary: |
      `executeMigrateShowPlan` takes a required `invocation` option, `{ cwd, configPath, dbGiven }`, like the control client's `migrate`: where the commands its advice prints are run from, the `--config` they repeat, and whether they repeat `--db`. Pass the same `invocation` you pass to `migrate`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '\bexecuteMigrateShowPlan\s*\('
  - id: marker-mismatch-meta
    summary: |
      The `meta` of `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH` no longer has `reachableHashes`. It has `spaceId`, `markerHash` and `targetHash`; `lastGraphHash`, the last contract in the migration graph the database applied, when its ledger shows one; and `missingMigrations`, the applied migrations after it that are no longer on disk, absent when the ledger could not be read. Code that read `reachableHashes` should read these fields, or show the error's `why` and `nextActions`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '\breachableHashes\b'
  - id: psl-temporal-type-renames
    summary: |
      On PostgreSQL, the PSL types `Timestamptz`, `Timestamp` and `Interval` are renamed to `TimestamptzTemporal`, `TimestampTemporal` and `IntervalParts`, and the old names are errors. Rename each use in your `.prisma` files, keeping its arguments: `Timestamptz(3)` becomes `TimestamptzTemporal(3)`. Each new name reads the same value with the same codec, so the contract and its hashes do not change. `@db.Timestamp` and `@db.Timestamptz` in a Prisma 7 schema are not affected.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.prisma"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$.@"\x27`])(?:Timestamptz|Timestamp|Interval)(?![\w$])'
  - id: ts-temporal-type-helpers-renamed
    summary: |
      In a TypeScript contract, `type.Timestamptz(...)`, `type.Timestamp(...)` and `type.Interval(...)` are renamed to `type.TimestamptzTemporal(...)`, `type.TimestampTemporal(...)` and `type.IntervalParts(...)`, and the column helper `intervalColumn(...)` from `@prisma/orm-postgres/adapter/column-types` is renamed to `intervalPartsColumn(...)`. Rename each call; the arguments do not change.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$])type\.(?:Timestamptz|Timestamp|Interval)\('
        - '(?<![\w$])intervalColumn(?![\w$])'
  - id: interval-with-precision-typed-as-parts
    summary: |
      An `IntervalParts(p)` column, an interval with a precision, is now typed as the `{ months, days, micros }` object its codec reads, as an interval without a precision already was, instead of a string. Type such a value as `PgInterval` from `@prisma/orm-postgres/target/codec-types`. Code that treated the value as a string was wrong at run time and now fails to type-check.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - 'import\s+(?:type\s+)?\{[^}]*(?<![\w$])Interval(?![\w$])[^}]*\}\s*from\s*[\x27"]@prisma/orm-postgres/(?:contract-builder|target/codec-types)[\x27"]'
  - id: branded-time-types-removed
    summary: |
      The string types `Timestamp`, `Timestamptz`, `Time` and `Interval` are no longer exported from `@prisma/orm-postgres/target/codec-types` (and `Interval` no longer from `@prisma/orm-postgres/contract-builder`). No column was typed by the first three. Remove each of these names from the import that names it, and delete the import if it names nothing else. An emitted `contract.d.ts` imports them without using them. Re-emit it with `prisma contract emit`; do not edit it by hand. Only a frozen copy in a migration snapshot, `migrations/snapshots/<hash>/contract.d.ts`, is never re-emitted: remove the names from its import by hand, and change nothing else in it.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - 'import\s+(?:type\s+)?\{[^}]*(?<![\w$])(?:Timestamptz|Timestamp|Time|Interval)(?![\w$])[^}]*\}\s*from\s*[\x27"]@prisma/orm-postgres/(?:contract-builder|target/codec-types)[\x27"]'
  - id: temporal-types-from-temporal-spec
    summary: |
      Temporal fields are now typed with the `Temporal` types of the `temporal-spec` package rather than a global `Temporal` declaration, so they are typed even in a project without the polyfill's global types. The values are the same and assign to and from the global types. A type test that requires a field to be exactly `Temporal.Instant` (or another `Temporal` type) from the global declarations now fails: add `temporal-spec` (`1.0.1`) to your development dependencies and import the type with `import type { Temporal } from 'temporal-spec'` in that test.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\s\S])(?![\s\S]*import\s+(?:type\s+)?\{[^}]*(?<![\w$])Temporal(?![\w$])(?!\s+as(?![\w$]))[^}]*\}\s*from\s*[\x27"]temporal-spec[\x27"])[\s\S]*toEqualTypeOf<\s*Temporal\.'
  - id: contract-types-list-new-aggregates
    summary: |
      Optional. An emitted `contract.d.ts` lists the aggregates of every codec in the stack, so `prisma contract emit` now adds rows for the three new codecs to it, and the contract itself does not change. Re-emit when you next change the contract; until then the existing `contract.d.ts` keeps working. A frozen `contract.d.ts` in a migration snapshot, `migrations/snapshots/<hash>/contract.d.ts`, is never re-emitted and does not need the new rows; it needs only the hand edit to its import that `branded-time-types-removed` describes.
  - id: iso-string-date-time-values
    summary: |
      The PostgreSQL text date and time types (`TimestamptzString`, `TimestampString`, `DateString`, `TimeString`, `Timetz`) read and write ISO 8601, the form the contract stores, instead of the text PostgreSQL prints. A `timestamptz` reads as the instant in UTC whatever the session's time zone, as in `2024-01-01T00:00:00Z`. A literal default or enum member on these types must be written in that form.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{prisma,ts,tsx,mts,cts,js,mjs,cjs}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$])(?:TimestamptzString|TimestampString|DateString|TimeString|Timetz)(?![\w$])'
        - '(?<![\w$])(?:timestamptzStringColumn|timestampStringColumn|dateStringColumn|timeStringColumn|timetzColumn|createdAtString|updatedAtString)(?![\w$])'
        - 'pg/(?:timestamptz-string|timestamp-string|date-string|time-string|timetz)@1'
  - id: date-style-iso-required
    summary: |
      The PostgreSQL driver ensures `DateStyle=ISO` on every connection it uses, including a `pg.Pool` or `pg.Client` the application passes to Prisma, which it sets with a statement. A statement in the application that sets a `DateStyle` other than `ISO`, or a pooler that drops the startup option, makes every read of a date or timestamp fail with `RUNTIME.DATE_STYLE_NOT_ISO`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,tsx,mts,cts,js,mjs,cjs,sql,env}"
      matches:
        - 'new\s+(?:pg\.)?(?:Pool|Client)\s*\('
        - '\b[Ss][Ee][Tt]\s+(?:[Ss][Ee][Ss][Ss][Ii][Oo][Nn]\s+|[Ll][Oo][Cc][Aa][Ll]\s+)?[Dd][Aa][Tt][Ee][Ss][Tt][Yy][Ll][Ee]\b'
        - '\b(?:[Dd][Aa][Tt][Ee][Ss][Tt][Yy][Ll][Ee]|PGDATESTYLE)\s*='
  - id: psl-field-presets-removed
    summary: |
      PSL field presets are removed. A field typed with a preset call, such as `id.uuidv4String()`, `nanoid({ size: 12 })`, `temporal.createdAt()` or `temporal.time(3, onUpdate: now)`, is refused with `PSL_UNRESOLVED_REFERENCE`, and the message gives the exact replacement. Rewrite each call as the tables in this guide say: a type constructor or a contributed alias, plus `@id`, `@onCreate(...)` and `@onUpdate(...)`. The contract does not change, so there is nothing to re-emit, sign or migrate. The detection matches schema files that type a field with a preset call.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.prisma"
      matches:
        - '(?:^|\n)[ \t]*\w+[ \t]+(?:temporal|id)\.[a-z]\w*[ \t]*\('
        - '(?:^|\n)[ \t]*\w+[ \t]+(?:text|int|bigint|float|decimal|boolean|json|bytes|dateTime|uuidString|uuidNative|ulid|nanoid|cuid2|ksuid)[ \t]*\('
  - id: ts-field-presets-removed
    summary: |
      The TypeScript contract builders have no field presets. `field.text()`, `field.uuidString()`, `field.json()` (on Postgres) and the other scalar presets, every `field.id.*` and every `field.temporal.*` no longer exist. TypeScript reports a missing property, and `prisma contract emit` on a contract that was not type-checked fails with `CONTRACT.FIELD_HELPER_UNKNOWN`, which names the rewrite. Rewrite each call as `field.column(type.X(...))` with `.id()`, `.onCreate(gen.fn())` and `.onUpdate(gen.fn())`, as the tables in this guide say, including the fields of query fragments. The contract does not change. MongoDB's `field.date()`, `field.string()`, `field.json()` and the other codec helpers are not presets and stay. The detection matches TypeScript files that call a preset; it matches a `field.json()` call only in a file that names `@prisma/orm-postgres`, so a Postgres file that imports its builder through a local module is not matched.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$.])field\.(?:id|temporal)\.'
        - '(?<![\w$.])field\.(?:text|int|bigint|float|decimal|boolean|bytes|dateTime|uuidString|uuidNative|ulid|nanoid|cuid2|ksuid)\('
        - '(?<![\s\S])(?=[\s\S]*@prisma/orm-postgres)[\s\S]*(?<![\w$.])field\.json\('
  - id: ts-field-generated-removed
    summary: |
      `field.generated(...)` and the spec helpers `uuidv4()`, `uuidv7()`, `ulid()`, `nanoid()`, `cuid2()` and `ksuid()` from `@prisma/orm-framework/ids` are removed. Write the identifier's type alias with `.onCreate(gen.fn())` instead, such as `field.column(type.Ulid()).onCreate(gen.ulid())`, as the table in this guide says, and remove the import. The contract does not change. The detection matches TypeScript files that call `field.generated` or import one of those helpers.
    detection:
      glob: "**/*.{ts,mts,cts,tsx}"
      matches:
        - '(?<![\w$.])field\.generated\('
        - 'import\s*(?:type\s*)?\{[^}]*(?<![\w$])(?:uuidv4|uuidv7|ulid|nanoid|cuid2|ksuid)(?![\w$])[^}]*\}\s*from\s*[\x27"]@prisma/orm-framework/ids[\x27"]'
  - id: postgres-contract-builder-exports-type
    summary: |
      No action is needed. `@prisma/orm-postgres/contract-builder` now exports `type` beside `field` and `gen`, the same type constructors and aliases the `defineContract` callback receives, so a query fragment declares a field as `field.column(type.TimestamptzTemporal())`.
  - id: sqlite-sql-char
    summary: |
      No action is needed. Every SQL target now has the type constructor `sql.Char(n)` in PSL and `type.sql.Char(n)` in TypeScript, which stores a fixed-length text column of `n` characters. On SQLite it is the only way to write a fixed-length text column, such as the column of a nanoid of another size.
  - id: identifier-type-aliases
    summary: |
      No action is needed. Every SQL target now has a type alias for the column of each identifier format the client generates: `sql.UuidString`, `sql.Ulid`, `sql.Nanoid`, `sql.Cuid2` and `sql.Ksuid` in PSL, and `type.sql.Ulid()` and the others in TypeScript. Postgres also names them at the top level, as `Ulid` and `type.Ulid()`. Each stores the same column as `Char(n)` of its length, so the identifier presets are rewritten with them.
  - id: prisma7-schema-now-default-writes-on-create
    summary: |
      A contract from `prisma7Schema(...)` now reads Prisma 7's `@default(now())` on a date or time field as both the database default `now()` and the client generator `now` on create, as Prisma 8 PSL reads `@default(now()) @onCreate(now())`. A create through Prisma 8 now writes the current UTC time, as Prisma 7's client did, instead of leaving the column to the database's clock in the session time zone. Re-emit the contract with `prisma contract emit` and commit it. Only the execution hash changes, so the database needs no migration and no `db sign`.
    detection:
      glob: "**/prisma.config.{ts,mts,cts,js,mjs}"
      matches:
        - '\bprisma7Schema\s*\('
  - id: contract-artifacts-restamp
    summary: |
      An extension that writes its own package version into the contracts it emits, such as the Supabase extension, now writes 8.0.0-rc.21. Run `contract emit` once after upgrading so the emitted `contract.json` and `contract.d.ts` match the installed extension.
    detection:
      glob: "**/contract.json"
      contains:
        - '"version": "8.0.0-rc.20"'
---

# 8.0.0-rc.20 → 8.0.0-rc.21 — User upgrade instructions

## Order of the steps

Do the steps in this order, and skip a step that does not apply to the project:

1. Upgrade the Prisma packages.
2. Change a MongoDB contract source as the MongoDB entries below say: pass the target pack to `mongoContract` (`mongo-contract-target-option`), rename the contract types (`mongo-contract-input`, `mongo-model-definition-removed`), and fix any discriminator, index or enum the contract now refuses (`mongo-ts-polymorphism-rules`, `mongo-index-shape-rules`, `mongo-value-object-enum-check`).
3. Change a PostgreSQL contract source: rename the date and time types (`psl-temporal-type-renames`, `ts-temporal-type-helpers-renamed`), remove the date and time types no longer exported from its imports (`branded-time-types-removed`), and write each literal default or enum member of a text date or time type in ISO 8601 (`iso-string-date-time-values`).
4. Rewrite every field preset and `field.generated(...)` in the contract sources and query fragments, with the type constructors, aliases and attributes the tables in "Field presets are removed" give (`psl-field-presets-removed`, `ts-field-presets-removed`, `ts-field-generated-removed`). Do this after step 3, because the tables use the new date and time type names.
5. Run `prisma contract emit` for every contract the project emits, and run it again with `--output-path` for each directory the project emits to that way (this also covers `contract-types-list-new-aggregates`, `prisma7-schema-now-default-writes-on-create` and `contract-artifacts-restamp`).
6. Run `prisma db sign` against every database when the project reads a Prisma 6 MongoDB schema whose storage hash changed (`mongo-prisma6-merged-indexes`).
7. On Postgres and SQLite, answer the question about a removed enum value the next time you run `migration plan` or `db update` (`removed-enum-value-questions`).
8. Change the application code: await client calls inside `try` blocks (`client-members-reject-instead-of-throwing`), stop using a runtime captured before `close()` (`close-ends-the-client-not-your-pool`), catch the connection error for a bad SQLite path (`sqlite-open-failure-is-a-connection-error`), pass `markerLocation` to `verifyContractSpaces` (`verify-contract-spaces-marker-location`), and, in code that calls the control API, drop `refuseMarkerOutsideGraph`, pass `invocation` to `executeMigrateShowPlan` and read the new `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH` fields (`refuse-marker-outside-graph-removed`, `execute-migrate-show-plan-requires-invocation`, `marker-mismatch-meta`).
9. Change the code that uses PostgreSQL date and time values: remove the date and time types no longer exported from the imports in your other source files and, by hand, in the frozen `contract.d.ts` copies under `migrations/snapshots/<hash>/`; every other `contract.d.ts` was re-emitted in step 5 (`branded-time-types-removed`, `interval-with-precision-typed-as-parts`), import `Temporal` from `temporal-spec` in type tests (`temporal-types-from-temporal-spec`), read text date and time values as ISO 8601 (`iso-string-date-time-values`), and remove any statement that sets a `DateStyle` other than `ISO` (`date-style-iso-required`).

## `mongoContract` takes the target pack

The MongoDB PSL contract source now builds its contract through the same builder `defineContract` uses, and that builder records the stack's target and extension packs. The source reads them from its options.

### `mongo-contract-target-option`

Pass the MongoDB target pack as `target`:

```typescript
import { mongoContract } from '@prisma/orm-family-mongo/contract-psl/provider';
import mongoTargetPack from '@prisma/orm-mongo/target/pack';

const contract = mongoContract('./prisma/schema.prisma', { target: mongoTargetPack });
```

Keep any other options you pass, such as `output`, in the same object. A config that names its contract through `defineConfig({ contract: './prisma/schema.prisma' })` from `@prisma/orm-mongo/config` already passes the pack. An app that calls `mongoContract` itself imports it from `@prisma/orm-family-mongo/contract-psl/provider`, so it depends on `@prisma/orm-family-mongo` as well as `@prisma/orm-mongo`; `@prisma/orm-mongo` does not export `mongoContract`. A call without `target` is refused with `CONTRACT.ARGUMENT_INVALID` (`reason: 'target-pack-missing'`).

## MongoDB contract types take SQL's names

Two MongoDB type names change so that they match SQL's. The types themselves do not change.

### `mongo-contract-input`

The type of the object you pass to `defineContract` is now `ContractInput`, as it is in SQL. Rename the import and each use:

```typescript
import type { ContractInput } from '@prisma/orm-mongo/contract-builder';
```

### `mongo-model-definition-removed`

`MongoModelDefinition` was an alias for a model of a built contract. SQL has no such alias. Write the type it stood for:

```typescript
import type { ContractModel } from '@prisma/orm-mongo/contract/types';
import type { MongoModelStorage } from '@prisma/orm-mongo/family-contract';

function collectionOf(model: ContractModel<MongoModelStorage>): string | undefined {
  return model.storage.collection;
}
```

## MongoDB contract sources share one builder

Every MongoDB contract source, `defineContract`, Prisma 8 PSL and the Prisma 6 reader, now builds through one builder, so each MongoDB rule applies to every source in the same way. The entries below are where a source now refuses or accepts what it did not before. A contract that every source accepted before builds to the same `contract.json`.

### `mongo-ts-polymorphism-rules`

The detection matches a file that imports the MongoDB contract builder and declares a discriminator; an emitted `contract.d.ts` imports no builder, so it is not matched.

A discriminator must be a required text field, and each variant must be declared and stored in its base's collection:

```typescript
const Task = model('Task', {
  collection: 'tasks',
  fields: { _id: field.objectId(), type: field.string() },
  discriminator: { field: 'type', variants: { Bug: { value: 'bug' } } },
});
const Bug = model('Bug', { base: Task, fields: { severity: field.int32() } });
```

### `mongo-index-shape-rules`

MongoDB refuses these indexes when it creates them, so the contract now refuses them first. A matched file uses a wildcard, a hashed key, a wildcard projection or a collation; check each such index against the list in the summary.

### `mongo-value-object-enum-check`

Declare every enum a value object field uses in `defineContract({ enums })`.

### `mongo-newly-accepted`

Nothing to change.

### `mongo-prisma6-merged-indexes`

Emit the contract again and sign the database, so `db verify` compares against the new storage hash.

## A removed enum value is asked about

### `removed-enum-value-questions`

If your contract removes a member of an enum, for example `ARCHIVED` from `Status`, the next `migration plan` or `db update` asks about it, as it asks about a model or field you remove: once, however many columns hold it.

If you renamed the member, give the rename, and the rows that held the old stored value hold the new one:

```bash
prisma db update --rename Status.ARCHIVED:Status.RETIRED
```

Otherwise the value is removed. A script that runs without a terminal fails with `CLI.CONSENT_REQUIRED`, naming the value. To let it go, add `--delete Status.ARCHIVED`: optional columns that hold it are set to NULL, and lists lose it. A required column cannot take NULL, so while rows of a required column hold the value, the apply fails with `MIGRATION.PRECHECK_FAILED`, changes nothing, counts the rows, and says how to keep them: rename the value to a new member, or keep that data by hand.

A member renamed with its stored value kept, for example with `RETIRED = "archived"`, changes nothing in the rows, and is not asked about. A member that keeps its name but stores a new value is asked about with `--delete` only, and so are two members that swap stored values; to keep the rows, the question names, for every column the enum types, the `this.removeStoredValue(...)` call to replace with `this.replaceStoredValue(...)` calls in the `migration.ts` that `migration plan` writes, and the `node` command that runs it. A swap goes through a temporary value. `db update` cannot keep that data in one run: its question says to plan the change with `migration plan --from <hash>`, or to rename the member to a new member and back in two runs of `db update`. For a swap only the plan works, and without migrations `db update` says it cannot keep the data.

Renames that shift stored values along, such as `Higher = 3` to `A = 4` while `Max = 4` becomes `B = 5`, are planned in one run, the last value first. Renames that move stored values in a cycle are refused; the refusal prints the `migration plan` command to write those rewrites by hand in, through a value no member stores.

Native Postgres enums (`pg.enum(...)`) are unchanged.

## A client reports failures through what its members return

### `client-members-reject-instead-of-throwing`

```ts
await db.close();

// Before: throws at the call, so .catch never runs
db.query(plan).toArray().catch(handle);

// After: the result rejects, so handle runs
db.query(plan).toArray().catch(handle);

// A synchronous try/catch around an unawaited call stops catching
try {
  db.transaction(work);
} catch (error) {
  handle(error);
}

// Await it instead
try {
  await db.transaction(work);
} catch (error) {
  handle(error);
}
```

## Postgres and SQLite errors are classified by code

### `close-ends-the-client-not-your-pool`

When you pass your own `pg.Pool` or `pg.Client` to `postgres()` or `supabase()`, `close()` on the Prisma client now also closes its runtime. Calls on `db` already failed after `close()`; what changes is a runtime you captured with `db.runtime()` before `close()`, which used to keep working and now refuses new work. Your pool or client is still yours: Prisma never ends it. If you used a captured runtime after `close()`, create a new Prisma client on the same pool instead:

```ts
await db.close();
const db2 = postgres({ contract, pg: pool });
```

A `pg.Client` you pass in may be connected or not: Prisma connects it if it has not started connecting. If its connection is lost, create a new `pg.Client`; a pg client cannot reconnect.

### `sqlite-open-failure-is-a-connection-error`

When the SQLite database file cannot be opened, the driver now raises a connection error (`SqlConnectionError`) instead of a query error (`SqlQueryError`).

## `verifyContractSpaces` names the marker location

### `verify-contract-spaces-marker-location`

A project that checks its contract spaces itself passes the marker location of its target to `verifyContractSpaces`, so the advice for an orphan marker names the right table:

```ts
// Before
verifyContractSpaces({ loadedSpaces, spaceDirsOnDisk, headRefsBySpace, markerRowsBySpace });

// After
verifyContractSpaces({
  loadedSpaces,
  spaceDirsOnDisk,
  headRefsBySpace,
  markerRowsBySpace,
  markerLocation: 'prisma_contract.marker',
});
```

The marker location is `prisma_contract.marker` on Postgres, `_prisma_marker` on SQLite and MySQL, and `_prisma_migrations` on MongoDB.

## The control API checks markers against the migration graph itself

These three changes affect only code that calls `@prisma/orm-toolchain/cli/control-api`. A project that runs the `prisma` CLI has nothing to change.

```ts
// Before
const refusal = refuseMarkerOutsideGraph({ markerHash, graph });
if (refusal) return notOk(refusal);
const plan = await executeMigrateShowPlan({ ...options });

// After: the operation returns MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH itself
const plan = await executeMigrateShowPlan({ ...options, invocation });
if (!plan.ok && plan.failure.code === 'MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH') {
  // plan.failure.meta: spaceId, markerHash, targetHash, lastGraphHash?, missingMigrations?
}
```

### `refuse-marker-outside-graph-removed`

For every file matched by `detection`, delete the call to `refuseMarkerOutsideGraph` and the handling of what it returned. `migrate` and `executeMigrateShowPlan` now make the same check for every contract space and return `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH` as their failure.

### `execute-migrate-show-plan-requires-invocation`

For every call matched by `detection`, add `invocation: { cwd, configPath, dbGiven }`, the same value the project passes to `migrate`. Set `dbGiven: true` when the project passes a database URL, so the printed commands include `--db <url>`.

### `marker-mismatch-meta`

For every file matched by `detection` that reads the `meta` of `MIGRATION.MARKER_MISMATCH`, read `spaceId`, `markerHash`, `targetHash`, `lastGraphHash` and `missingMigrations` instead of `reachableHashes`, or show the error's `why` and `nextActions`. `MIGRATION.HASH_NOT_IN_GRAPH` still has `reachableHashes`; leave code that reads it there unchanged.

The error's text changes too. `prisma db migrate` now prints `The database's marker names <hash>, which no migration in <directory> starts or ends at.`, followed by what the database applied after the last contract of the graph it reached. Its next actions give two recoveries, `prisma db update` for a database whose migration history does not need to be kept, and new migrations for one that changes only through migrations. None of them resets the database.

## Explicit date and time types carry the kind of value they read

On PostgreSQL, a column type that several codecs read now names the kind of value in its name. The `Temporal` types gain the suffix `Temporal`, and the interval type that reads `{ months, days, micros }` gains the suffix `Parts`:

| Before | After | Reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Timestamptz(p?)` | `TimestamptzTemporal(p?)` | `Temporal.Instant` |
| `Timestamp(p?)` | `TimestampTemporal(p?)` | `Temporal.PlainDateTime` |
| `Interval(p?)` | `IntervalParts(p?)` | `{ months, days, micros }` |

This change leaves `DateTime`, `Date` and `Time` as they are, and adds `DateTemporal` and `TimeTemporal` as the explicit names of what `Date` and `Time` read today. A later release gives `DateTime`, `Date` and `Time` new meanings, as convenience date and time types, and brings its own instructions. To keep what a field reads today through that change, you can already write the explicit name: `TimestamptzTemporal` for `DateTime`, `DateTemporal` for `Date` and `TimeTemporal` for `Time`.

Three explicit types are new, and need no change to existing schemas: `TimestampJsDate(p?)`, a `timestamp` column read as a JavaScript `Date`; `TimestampInstant(p?)`, a `timestamp` column read as a `Temporal.Instant`; and `IntervalString(p?)`, an `interval` column read as an ISO 8601 duration such as `P1Y2M`. Both timestamp types read and write the stored date and time as UTC.

### `psl-temporal-type-renames`

Rename each field type in your `.prisma` files using the table above, keeping its arguments and its attributes:

```prisma
model Event {
  id    Int                    @id
  at    TimestamptzTemporal(3) // was Timestamptz(3)
  local TimestampTemporal      // was Timestamp
  span  IntervalParts          // was Interval
}
```

A type alias written with one of the names, such as `types { Stamp = Timestamp(3) }`, is renamed the same way. The detection can match one of the words in a comment or a model name; rename only a field type or an alias's type.

### `ts-temporal-type-helpers-renamed`

```ts
field.column(type.TimestamptzTemporal(3)); // was type.Timestamptz(3)
field.column(intervalPartsColumn(6)); // was intervalColumn(6)
```

### `interval-with-precision-typed-as-parts`

```ts
import type { PgInterval } from '@prisma/orm-postgres/target/codec-types';

const span: PgInterval = row.span; // an IntervalParts(6) column
```

### `branded-time-types-removed`

In source files you wrote, remove the four names from the import. Re-emit every emitted `contract.d.ts` with `prisma contract emit` instead of editing it. The only `contract.d.ts` files to edit by hand are the frozen copies in migration snapshots, `migrations/snapshots/<hash>/contract.d.ts`, which are never re-emitted. In those, remove the four names from the import and leave the rest of the file as it is:

```ts
import type {
  CodecTypes as PgTypes,
  JsonValue,
} from '@prisma/orm-postgres/target/codec-types'; // was also importing Interval, Time, Timestamp and Timestamptz
```

### `temporal-types-from-temporal-spec`

```ts
import type { Temporal } from 'temporal-spec';

expectTypeOf<Row['createdAt']>().toEqualTypeOf<Temporal.Instant>();
```

If the test file also creates `Temporal` values, import the type under another name, such as `import type { Temporal as TemporalTypes } from 'temporal-spec'`, so the runtime `Temporal` stays in scope.

### `contract-types-list-new-aggregates`

No change is needed now. The next `prisma contract emit` adds rows for the three new codecs to `contract.d.ts`.

## Text date and time values are ISO 8601

### `iso-string-date-time-values`

A column of `TimestamptzString`, `TimestampString`, `DateString`, `TimeString` or `Timetz` used to read the text PostgreSQL prints, which depends on the session's `TimeZone` and `DateStyle`. It now reads ISO 8601, the same on every server:

| Type | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TimestamptzString` | `2024-01-01 01:00:00+01` on a server in `Europe/Berlin` | `2024-01-01T00:00:00Z` |
| `TimestampString` | `2024-01-01 12:34:56.5` | `2024-01-01T12:34:56.5` |
| `DateString`, 44 BC | `0044-03-15 BC` | `-000043-03-15` |
| `Timetz` | `12:34:56+02`, `12:34:56+00` | `12:34:56+02:00`, `12:34:56Z` |

The same text is read inside an `.include()`. `infinity` and `-infinity` are unchanged. The generated `now()` values of these columns, such as `temporal.UpdatedAtString`, are written in the same form.

Change the code that reads these values:

- Code that parses the old text, for example by replacing the space with `T` or appending `Z` before `new Date(...)`, can pass the value to `new Date(...)` or `Temporal.Instant.from(...)` directly for a `TimestamptzString`. A `TimestampString` value has no offset; append `Z` to read it as UTC, as before.
- Code that compares a read value with text in the old form, in application code or in tests, compares with the ISO form.
- Code that shows a value to a user formats it for display, since the value is no longer in the session's time zone.

A value the application writes may still be in any form PostgreSQL reads, and it reads back in ISO 8601. A literal default or an enum member on these types must be written in the stored form, because Prisma compares it with the value a query returns:

```ts
// Before
scheduledAt: field.column(timestamptzStringColumn).default('2024-01-15 10:30:00+00'),

// After
scheduledAt: field.column(timestamptzStringColumn).default('2024-01-15T10:30:00Z'),
```

`contract emit` refuses a default in another form with `CONTRACT.DEFAULT_INVALID`, and the message shows the form to write. A PSL default written with a tag, such as `` @default(timestamptz`2024-01-15 10:30:00+00`) ``, is unchanged. An enum on `TimestampString`, `TimestamptzString` or `Timetz` is now allowed.

The `now()` value of a `TimestampString(p)` or `TimestamptzString(p)` column is now rounded down to the column's precision, as a time column's is, so the column stores the value generated. Emit the contract again: its execution hash changes where such a column has a `now()` generator.

### `date-style-iso-required`

The PostgreSQL driver now ensures `DateStyle=ISO` on every connection it uses. A connection Prisma opens from a URL starts with it as a startup option, after any `options` in the URL or `PGOPTIONS`. On a `pg.Pool` or `pg.Client` you pass to Prisma, the driver sets it with one statement on each connection before first use, and again after a connection held for a transaction, an ORM operation or a Supabase role scope is released. Nothing needs changing for either.

Remove any statement that sets a `DateStyle` other than `ISO` on a connection Prisma uses, such as a `SET DateStyle` in a pool's `connect` handler or in raw SQL: every date and time codec that reads a date or timestamp (text, `Temporal` or `Date`) refuses text in another style with `RUNTIME.DATE_STYLE_NOT_ISO`. Behind a connection pooler that refuses startup options, pass Prisma your own `pg.Pool` instead of a URL; behind one that runs each statement on another server connection, also run `ALTER ROLE <role> SET DateStyle = 'ISO'` (or set it on the database).

## Field presets are removed

This section replaces two pieces of advice from the 8.0.0-rc.19 upgrade guide. That guide said that `field.generated(...)` keeps working for now, and that a field preset keeps its `number`, `option` and `object` arguments. Neither holds any more: this release removes `field.generated(...)` and every field preset, in PSL and in TypeScript, and the tables below give what to write instead.

A field preset was a call in a field's type position that set the column, the identity and the generated values at once, such as `id.uuidv4String()` or `temporal.createdAt()`. Each is now written with what the rest of a contract uses: a type constructor or a contributed alias, such as `Ulid` or `temporal.CreatedAt`, plus `@id`, `@onCreate(...)` and `@onUpdate(...)` in PSL, or `.id()`, `.onCreate(gen.fn())` and `.onUpdate(gen.fn())` in TypeScript. Every replacement stores the same contract as its preset, with the same storage and execution hashes. So after the rewrite nothing is re-emitted, signed or migrated: `prisma contract emit` writes the `contract.json` you have. Rewrite the calls where your project's comments and documentation show them too, such as a README, in PSL and in TypeScript; the detections look only at `.prisma` and TypeScript files.

```prisma
// Before
model Event {
  id        id.uuidv4String()
  code      nanoid({ size: 12 })
  seenAt    temporal.time(3, onUpdate: now)
  createdAt temporal.createdAt()
  payload   json()
}

// After
model Event {
